subsubtopic: CALL FOR EXTENSION OF EXPIRY DATE OF DEVELOPMENT BOND-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Whereas the government has only recently introduced the small business development bond legislation, which now has an amended termination date of April 1, 1981, and there is very little time left for the vitally important small business sector in Canada to take advantage of any benefit under the bonds, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling):
That this House urge the government to extend the expiry date of the small business development bond to December 31, 1981.

speechtext:

Recent reports indicate a serious threat to the health of Canadians, as evidenced by the marked increase among Canadians of tropical and other exotic diseases such as the tenfold increase in malaria during the past five years. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Don Valley West (Mr. Bosley):
That (he Flouse encourage the Minister of National Health and Welfare to direct special attention to the problem of tropical and exotic diseases in Canada, including the concept of an institute of tropical medicine.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO NORTHERN RESIDENTS TO MEET INCREASED COSTS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. If anyone doubts that we are in an economic crisis, they should look north where inflation is rampant. As of January 5, 1981, in Gjoa Haven, Northwest Territories, eggs cost $4.30 a dozen, bread cost $2.65 a loaf and two kilograms of powdered milk cost $8.50. Considering that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is perhaps more sympathetic to problems of isolation since his experience in Lech, letching for avocados, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae):
That this government take immediate steps to ensure that northerners are able to obtain nutritionally valuable food at Canadian prices.

subsubtopic: "TORONTO SUN"-REFERENCE TO "GIRLS FROM PARLIAMENT HILL"-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, which I know members on all sides of the House will support. Yesterday, January 14, on page 50 of The Toronto Sun, there was an advertisement for the Hotel Brampton presented by the
Centrefold Model & Entertainment Agency, which says in part "Hotel Brampton Presents The Girls from Parliament Hill". Madam Speaker, this advertisement is an embarrassment to Parliament Hill. In my opinion it constitutes false advertising and it is a direct insult to the integrity of the women who work on Parliament Hill. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis):
That the Speaker of the House of Commons undertake an investigation into this matter and, if it is found that the advertising is not accurate, that appropriate action be taken by the Speaker and a public apology be given to the women who work on Parliament Hill by the Hotel Brampton and the Centrefold Model & Entertainment Agency.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Whereas the Minister of Labour (Mr. Regan), who is responsible for fitness and amateur sport, recently withdrew funding from various native recreation and cultural programs without supplying any alternatives for these programs, and whereas these programs employ native people and the disruption of these programs has the potential of intensifying social problems within Canada's native communities, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga):
That this government take immediate action to maintain existing programs and their personnel and accept native fitness and amateur sport in the same priority and on the same basis that all other Canadians enjoy.

subsubtopic: EFFECTS OF PROGRAM ON INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the minister of energy and it deals with his national energy policy. In spite of the evidence, which is
Oral Questions
mounting daily, that the minister's energy policy is a disaster for Canada, the minister stated in the House yesterday and also last Monday that he has no intention of changing that policy. In contrast, prior to Christmas the minister and the Prime Minister said at least a dozen times in this House that they were willing to negotiate with the provinces, the industry or both.
Given the now documented proof that his policy is causing the departure of dozens and dozens of rigs and millions, if not billions, of dollars, the loss of jobs on a large scale and jeopardizing of the nation's security in oil, can the minister tell the House why he has taken this new, rigid position? Is it a matter of pride, or is he not aware of just what damage his policy is causing?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: EFFECTS OF PROGRAM ON INDUSTRY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 would remind the hon. member that on the contrary the object of the policy we have announced is to maintain the growth rate of inflation at an acceptable level and prevent it from rising to such high levels as those which now plague a great many industrialized countries. In addition our policy is aimed at preserving tens of thousands of jobs which would vanish because of unduly rapid increases in oil prices. That is substantiated again if we look at what is going on in a great many other advanced countries. Indeed the government and I have indicated quite clearly that we were prepared to negotiate in good faith with industry spokesmen and particularly with the Alberta government. I must point out to the hon. member that the government has already amended some of the budget proposals, especially as regards exploration wells, and that certain measures will be deferred until next year, in 1982. Besides, we have already made it clear that we were quite willing to meet with Alberta government representatives at the ministerial level or at the official level. The government in Edmonton has until now refused to meet at the ministerial level but again I say that we are available. I must point out that the government is firmly committed to reach the objectives we set for ourselves in the energy program but I must say that we did show flexibility in the implementation of that program.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Since the Government of Canada seconded the UN resolution declaring 1981 to be the International Year of the Disabled, will the minister tell the House, and more importantly tell 700,000 disabled Canadians, why they have allocated only $1 million to projects for the handicapped this year, which represents a financial contribution of something less than $1.50 per disabled Canadian?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: FUNDING OF PROJECTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I take the question of the hon. member more as a representation in favour of the handicapped. We all support and share the responsibility for the handicapped including provinces, municipalities and other institutions in the country.
The government has put aside the $1 million which the hon. member has referred to for projects which communities or groups will present to the organizing committee in Canada. The provinces are also putting aside a similar budget. It is not identical because it will depend on the order of magnitude and what possibilities present themselves in each province. That does not preclude our departments of health and welfare across the country, or other departments in the various provinces, from having ongoing projects.
Very soon the federal government will announce projects for each department. We are expecting a report from the committee on which the hon. member sits; it has not been made public yet, although we expected it at the beginning of the year.

subsubtopic: POLICY RESPECTING SETTING OF PRIME RATE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question today is directed to the Minister of Finance. The minister will know that as a result of the auction today, the Bank of Canada rate is still within a whisker of 17 per cent, having gone down the magnificent amount of three-one hundredths of 1 per cent. The minister has organized his Bank of Canada rate on the basis of one-quarter per cent over the treasury bill rate. The minister auctioned off $1,310 billion of treasury bills. His 182 bills sold at 15.3 per cent. His one-year bills sold out at 14.4 per cent.
Why will the minister not direct the Bank of Canada to determine its rate on the basis of its average sale of treasury bills-for example, on a sale of treasury bills at 15.4 per cent-to give a Bank of Canada rate of 15.65 per cent, instead of insisting on using the highest rate to determine the Bank of Canada rate and, therefore, forcing the base rate of interest in this country to be higher than it should be?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: POLICY RESPECTING SETTING OF PRIME RATE
speechtext:

Madam Speaker, the question really relates to a much broader problem. Indeed, there is a shortage of nurses right across Canada and the situation is particularly acute in eastern Canada. We are facing at the present time a dilemma between the tremendous movement of nurses to the United States and to the western part of this country, leaving extreme shortages in hospitals in eastern Canada because of the cutbacks in training which took place three or four years ago.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, may 1 put a question to the government House leader regarding the House business for next week? As the government House leader must know, it used to be a tradition, when a prime minister or a secretary of state for external affairs came back to Canada from trips to other countries, that automatically a statement was made in the House. In recent times that tradition seems to have been dropped, yet I wonder if the government does not realize the importance of the North-South dialogue. Will the government House leader impress upon the Prime Minister very seriously the point suggested by the hon. member for Saskatoon East that some day next week there might be a formal statement by the Prime Minister on his North-South discussions so that there can then be responses from this side of the House?
I realize there is the usual comment that we have opposition days, but surely this is a matter of concern to the government and the whole country, and it ought to be worth a statement by the Prime Minister and responses to that statement.

subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my hon. colleague understands very well that under the provisions of Standing Order 15(3) the Prime Minister does not have to make such a statement. On the other hand, he will understand that the Prime Minister has always been happy in the past and will be happy to answer questions on the subject almost every day during oral question period.

subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
Moreover, 1 am sure the Prime Minister will be happy to participate, directly or indirectly, in any debate on one of the allotted days as the hon. member just mentioned which are available to the opposition parties. I think this would be much more useful for the country than spreading some kind of panic regarding the economy when there is no reason to spread such panic, as his party did in the last few days.
I suggest that the hon. member should use question period and maybe one or two of the allotted days available to the opposition. If he undertakes to do that, I will be very happy to suggest to the Prime Minister that he consider seriously the possibility of making the statement about which the member talked. But we will take into consideration the time taken during question period on this subject, and if it has not been covered sufficiently during question period, perhaps then the Prime Minister will be happy to make a statement.
My hon. colleague just recognized that it is not an obligation, but on the other hand he will also agree the opposition will have many opportunities to ask questions of the Prime Minister on this subject. I am sure the Prime Minister will be very pleased to provide the opposition with all the answers he is willing to give them.

subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we both understand the rules of the House and the obligations and privileges of the Prime Minister, but surely this subject is of such great importance that it ought not to be one on which the government waits for questions to which to respond. Surely it is a question on which the government should take the lead.
The government House leader has already promised that he will speak to the Prime Minister about this matter, but I hope he will put his weight as House leader behind the proposition that the Prime Minister ought to take the initiative of making a statement on motions so that, on the government's initiative, we can have a discussion of this important issue.

subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise on the same question. It is really generated most recently by the comments of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre concerning the practices of the House. We have seen a quite regular and a much more frequent recourse to the use of closure by the government than had been the custom in the past. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre indicated, apparently we now have a deliberate departure from the practice of prime ministerial statements on major trips undertaken while Parliament is sitting, at public expense, and presumably in the interest of public policy. In the past those have been the cause for statements on motions, of report by a prime minister on his return.
There was a rather soft undertaking to discuss the matter but a very hard indication that it was the view of the government House leader that he would prefer to have the traditions of this place changed, to have the only responsibility by the Prime Minister evidenced through questions, through the response to questions or through an allotted opposition day.
On at least two occasions earlier today matters were dealt with which obviously would have been better dealt with through statements on motions. The Secretary of State and Minister of Communications, in failing to answer a question by my colleague, gave a long statement of government broadcasting policy which should have been made on a statement on motions. The Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment, in his capacity as government envoy on the constitutional matters, indicated today that there had not been the full and complete reporting to the House of Commons which the House of Commons had the right to expect as a result of the consultations in Great Britain in the autumn concerning the legislative timetable of Westminster and the matters before this House.
I apologize for the long preamble to my question, but we are seeing a number of reforms and changes in parliamentary procedure by the government acting unilaterally. The government House leader will recall that the government I had the honour to lead brought in a comprehensive program of parliamentary reform.
Does the government intend simply to change the practices of Parliament by unilateral action, or is it preparing a comprehensive program of parliamentary reform which will be
January 15, 1981

brought before the House so that we can consider deliberately how we want to change this Chamber, taking account of some of the excellent suggestions made the other day during the closure motion debate by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, taking account of the proposals put forward by my colleague and seatmate when he occupied the position of government House leader, and taking account of the very serious concerns about the adequency of parliamentary procedure felt by private members on all sides of the House? Will we have a full and comprehensive public, detailed proposal, or will we simply have the House traditions changed bit by bit unilaterally by the government?
[ Translation]

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, of course 1 do not expect the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition to think that 1 agree with his introductory remarks because they are highly politicized and do not reflect reality at all. But still the essence of his question is serious. That is why I will go along and answer because it has to do with parliamentary reform. But when he talks about breaking with tradition, Madam Speaker, it should be recalled that it was not the government which sent hon. members performing gymnastics before the Speaker of the House on the eve of a vote last fall when we were compelled and forced by the opposition to put an end to the debate which had been far too long.
Nor was it the government which today put a question to a minister, a question altogether foreign to his ministerial responsibilities. The Minister of the Environment replied out of courtesy, because we on this side of the House are very polite and quite prepared to overlook the procedural mistakes often made by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition. So I want to set things in their proper perspective and suggest that the traditions of this House are being changed not so much by members on this side of the House as by hon. members opposite, in the two cases I have just mentioned.
As to the application of Standing Order 15(3) concerning ministerial statements the Leader of the Opposition knows full well that we are not compelled to make any and that we make some now and again when hon. members have no opportunity to put questions to ministers on certain subjects, say a new policy for example, or if during oral question period it was impossible to question a minister or the Prime Minister on a given topic.
In this instance, the Prime Minister will be in the House next week. There will be a daily oral question period as usual and of course hon. members will be able to put questions to the Prime Minister who will have an opportunity to reply. If it becomes obvious that his answers are not satisfactory or that the Prime Minister does not have enough time to give all the answers required to enlighten the House and the Parliament of Canada about his trip to foreign countries, then I am convinced that he will indeed consider the advisability of following
Business of the House
the Standing Orders of the House to give more details to hon. members, either under the provisions of Standing Order 15(3) or in a statement, or again by offering his contribution during an allotted day when the opposition would have selected his trip as subject for debate. As I said earlier, the opposition will have at least six days to raise that subject if it so wishes. As to the substance of the question on parliamentary reform, of course it is important to think about it. Some traditions must be respected, others must disappear. I have said again and again that any change that might be made here will have been the object of discussions among members on both sides of the House. As far as I know, that process has been under way since I first came to this House in 1974, because our Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization has studied this question and tabled three reports on which no action was taken. And then we have the report introduced by the Progressive Conservative Party when they were in office and which features challenging ideas and other proposals that could stand revamping.
Other aspects of parliamentary reform deserve consideration since they flow from the recommendations of the Lambert report or of reports now on the order paper and issued by the Standing Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments. They must all be reviewed as a whole. Once we have all the elements I think we will be in a position, within reasonable time, to come up with suggestions and arrange to have them discussed by all parliamentarians.
But it is obvious that parliamentary reform has become necessary and urgent if this institution is to reflect reality. What does "reflect reality" mean? Very simply, enabling Parliament to adopt enough legislation to meet current needs-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext: -adopt enough legislation?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
-adopt enough legislation to meet current needs.
1 am answering the question seriously. I hope the right hon. gentleman will deign to listen because this is not a light subject.
To this day and for reasons which may be humanitarian but which we should not have to endure, the opposition has not been altogether co-operative in the adoption of legislation since Parliament resumed last fall. Unfortunate though it may be, it is the truth. Of course, we deal with consequential issues but it is also essential for the government to shoulder its responsibilities.
It was in that spirit, Madam Speaker, that earlier this week we were forced to serve notice that we would limit the debate, not impose closure as the Leader of the Opposition so liberally claims, but limit the debate. Why were we forced to limit the debate? Because the opposition parties did not want to hear anything about a reasonable length of time. Contrary to the

January 15, 1981
Business of the House
statement of the Leader of the Opposition, we could not possibly decide unilaterally to limit the debate without first consulting the opposition parties and offer them an opportunity to explain to us what they think is a reasonable length of time. We asked them if they wanted to sit down with us and tell us what would be reasonable as additional time to debate Bill C-48 on second reading. They said no, so we did not have any choice.
Parliamentary reform is necessary. Why? Precisely because we had constitutional problems in 1980 and now in 1981 we must come to grips with energetic and economic issues. Madam Speaker, we now have on the order paper 40-odd items about which the government must take action to answer the expectations of the people. And all of a sudden the opposition parties decide to filibuster, so we are expected to let them take over and manage the business of Parliament while we stand idly by. If we were to agree to play that game we would simply be giving up on the responsibilities which the majority of Canadians entrusted to us in the last election.
One thing I want to make clear to the Leader of the Opposition is that we do want to co-operate with members across the floor. We are prepared to discuss with them. We are prepared to sit down and talk over a reasonable schedule to implement a legislative program which will command respect for Parliament from all Canadians, so that we can show to the people that we have here men and women who can govern the country in an orderly and rational manner while respecting the full rights of the opposition to voice exhaustive but certainly not dilatory criticism. If in my capacity as government House leader I were to let the opposition have a field day with dilatory tactics I would be falling far short of assuming the responsibilities given to us by the Canadian people.
I suggest I would not be doing the opposition a service, I would be doing my share to destroy this institution. 1 am convinced that that is not the intent of the Leader of the Opposition but I remind him that the best way to prove that indeed he seeks what is best for this institution is to be more co-operative and refrain from filibustering. We on this side are quite willing to sit down and negotiate and to that end we are prepared to set aside every other political consideration. All we want is to respect the obligations of a modern government facing a modern opposition, but in an orderly manner.
When we realize that for partisan motives the opposition will not co-operate, then we are forced to use the Standing Orders of the House and, in this instance since my colleague refers directly to the events of this week, to resort to Standing Order 75C. In conclusion. Madam Speaker, I cannot refrain from recalling publicly that Standing Order 75C is a rule of the House and that it has nothing to do with unilateral action on the part of the government. Standing Order 75C cannot be applied and, as government House leader, I have no authority to limit the debate without first offering to the opposition
parties an opportunity to negotiate with us over what is a reasonable length of time.
That is an obligation which is spelled out in the Standing Orders and I went along with it but members opposite refused to negotiate a reasonable delay concerning the length of second reading of Bill C-48. Given such obvious and systematic obstruction we were forced to assume our responsibilities. We are hoping, Madam Speaker, that in future the opposition will not force us to act that way again.
Again I express publicly our will to co-operate with hon. members opposite and grant reasonable time for debate but it has become imperative, as the Leader of the Opposition wishes to change the Standing Orders, to launch parliamentary reform so that Parliament will be modern and efficient and reflect reality. Right now we are not doing anything more than attempting to do just that and to respect fully the obligations entrusted to us by the Canadian public and the people of Canada.

What I am saying is that these reports refer to the regulations which are linked very closely to parliamentary reform. In our view it is very important that these reports be considered at the same time as parliamentary reform. We would prefer to have these reports sent in due time to those who will be looking into parliamentary reform. subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to remind this House that how this whole debate began, and then wandered into closure, statutory instruments and all over the lot, was with a simple question on upcoming House business and whether or not the Prime Minister would be prepared to make a statement in the House on motions on his trip. 1 am aware that the Prime Minister has no obligation and that there is no rule requiring him to make such a statement.
We know that the government House leader cannot commit the Prime Minister at this point. All we want from the government House leader is an indication that he will ask or that he will somehow urge the Prime Minister with regard to this matter.
One of the most enlightening and interesting experiences for myself as a new member when I came to this House some years ago was statements on motions made by ministers. It was participatory democracy for the critics of the various areas, and it was extremely helpful. As observed by the Leader of the Opposition, that practice has greatly declined. Instead, we get ministers making what used to be statements on motions regarding policy and new departures and new procedures outside the House, or outside Room 130-S. 1 would urge the Prime Minister and other ministers to return at least partially to the practice of making statements on motions on important issues.

I would like to rule now on the question of privilege which was raised on Tuesday by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald). I listened very closely to all the arguments and the interventions made by the minister and by the hon. member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Miss Jewett) during the debate. I did not quite know what she meant when she was alluding to a mole and I was a bit nervous, not wanting to get up at every moment. It appeared that she was getting very close to saying something that was unparliamentary. I am sure that I interrupted her flight of oratory and I am sorry for that, but those were my reasons.
I feel we have taken the subject as far as we can under the heading of a question of privilege.

I refer first of all to question No. 136 which was placed on the order paper last April. It concerns the rental of a DC-9 aircraft by the Liberal Party of Canada which has not paid its bill to Air Canada for the use of that aircraft. It asks if Air Canada has received payment and, if so, when and how much did they receive. It seems pretty straightforward, but it is almost a year since that question was placed on the order paper.
I refer also to question No. 115 which inquires in a broader sense, in regard to the election campaign of February 18, 1980, what political parties rented aircraft from Air Canada, what they paid, if the bills were paid, etc. It is a very simple question, yet it has gone unanswered since the beginning of the session last April.
1 find it hard to accept that these questions remain unanswered after hearing the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) say a few minutes ago that he believed in responsibility toward the Canadian people and that that is why he wanted progress on the items on the order paper. If he does, why does he or his parliamentary secretary not answer these questions a little faster? He also said that he was willing to set aside all political concerns in regard to major items on the order paper. I think he should be prepared to set aside political concerns in regard to questions placed on the order paper by the elected representatives of the people. We have a right to know, as the people of Canada have, what the answers to these questions are.
May I conclude by referring to another series of questions, without going into detail. Question No. 29 concerning Michael Pitfield and the Taschereau papers on national security; ques-

speechtext: The House resumed, from Tuesday, January 13, 1981, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-48, to regulate oil and gas interests in Canada lands and to amend the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to resume debate in opposition to Bill C-48. I am also pleased to see that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) is here so that he can hear some of the environmental concerns which have been expressed to me by people around the country in relation to Bill C-48, even though we are not being given much time to debate it.
When I began speaking on Tuesday night, 1, along with many other members of this House, eastern, western and northern maritime Canadians, were under the illusion that the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) had their portfolios of public interest entrenched in Bill C-48.
It is abundantly clear that the Minister of the Environment may not long uphold his parliamentary and Crown responsibility to keep the environmental moratorium in place on the west coast. I think that became quite clear as a result of questions I raised yesterday during question period both with him and with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Much worse though, he and the Minister of Fisheries and
January 15, 1981

Oceans have failed totally to incorporate the sound policies put forward to them by their own respective departments.
1 shall quote briefly from a study done by the Department of Fisheries and the Department of the Environment called "A Study of Environmental Concerns-Offshore Oil and Gas Drilling and Production." 1 am sure the minister of energy is aware of this but.he went to great lengths to keep some of the concerns raised for those two ministers out of Bill C-48.
Some of the concerns found on page iv of this document are:
Toxic compounds are used in drilling fluids without justification.
Effluent controls are developed and applied unevenly in offshore areas.
Impact assessments of effluent discharges are inadequate.
Operators sometimes do not deal realistically with the spill containment and clean-up problems likely to be encountered.
Field testing of containment and clean-up equipment and procedures is often inadequate.
Oil spill liability and compensation provisions are inadequate.
I will deal with that specifically later on. I know the minister of energy is touting the absolute liability section as being the main way of dealing with this issue, and 1 have some interesting comments to make about that.
The concerns listed continue:
Most offshore drilling and production accidents, including spills, are caused by human error, yet efforts to respond to the situation are unorganized both in Canada and United States.
Safety and anti-pollution equipment is being used without standards; those that exist are written in excessively general terms.
1 might comment about this latter one. 1 have seen the Neels program. 1 notice that some areas supposedly in possession of large quantities of oil-spill equipment list it right down to having two or three pairs of gum boots, and having toilet paper on hand.
The concerns listed in this study continue:
Standards for old equipment are lacking. Data on failed equipment are lacking. Detailed logistical and environmental information on relief well drilling capabilities are often not provided by operators.
Logistical provisions which could reduce the relief well drilling time are often not made. Environmental impact assessment information is often collected with little or no clear idea of how it can or will be used to influence those who make the decisions regarding offshore oil and gas drilling and production operations.
1 would remind the Minister of Energy that he has specifically written the bill entirely into his own hands and, in an occasional situation, to his cabinet.
The next concern:
People having environmental concerns or expertise (including the public-at-large) are not given effective access to the policy and decision-making processes of regulatory authorities.
1 am sure the minister is well aware that the regulatory authority is himself basically in cabinet. The concerns continue with:
The lead time for conducting environmental assessments is too short. Many proponents provide only a superficial, unevaluated review of the impact literature; they do not seek to profit from the environmental mistakes already made by coastal zone developers around the world.
Canada Oil and Gas Act
I would draw the minister's attention to the fact that there is absolutely nothing in the bill to deal with very serious blowouts such as the Ixtoc blowout in the Gulf of Mexico last year.
The concerns continue:
Proponents draw inappropriate analogies between the proposed project and ones that have already been carried out and fail to uncover gaps in the literature. Acreage releases are not planned over the long term to provide a focus for environmental assessment work.
Information on sensitive areas is either not presented in impact assessments or is left unlinked to key decisions relating to offshore oil and gas activities. Development plans for production rigs do not make provisions for outside review. The environmental assessment requirements in the draft Canada Oil and Gas Production Regulations do not indicate how assessment results are to be linked with the key decision milestones involved in offshore production.
There is no reference to the federal Environmental Assessment and Review Process in the draft production regulations.
I would draw that one particularly to the minister's attention. It is of concern to environmentalists around this country. The minister pointedly made sure that that reference was not in Bill C-48.
The concerns continue:
There is no requirement that proponents provide alternative pipeline routes to shore in their development plans or that these alternatives be considered by the public and by others having environmental concerns.
Problems encountered in the United States and the North Sea during the development and production phases of offshore operations have not been adequately addressed in this country.
Those concerns are just in the first couple of pages of this report.
In my view the Minister of Energy has gutted the Minister of the Environment and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans of their responsibilities. If they have any intention of having credibility on maritime issues in Canada, they had better attend committee meetings, at least, beginning next week, and assure that amendments are made and passed to deal with those items I have listed and with those that no doubt will be raised by witnesses in the coming days. At this point 1 will certainly put the Minister of Energy on notice that our party intends to pursue the statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) acting as Deputy Prime Minister, that we will be allowed to call as many witnesses as we please on Bill C-48. We certainly intend to do that.
Surely it is the role of the opposition to map out weaknesses. However, there is a public responsibility that has not to date been upheld by these two particular ministers of the Crown. They have at their fingertips intelligent, scientific expertise that has been muzzled in the interests of partisan industrial expediency.
What is offered and clear for all Canadians to see is a blueprint for environmental disaster, the destruction, perhaps by insignificant increment, but ultimately the biological disruption of Canada's marine environment-as a direct result of failing to legislate, not to regulate, not to force British Columbians, maritimers, and northern Canadians to come and beg the Minister of Energy for the proper environmental studies, and that the proper studies be legislated and a sound regime for offshore oil and gas be put in place in Bill C-48.

January 1 5, 1981
Canada OH and Gas Act
I have here The National Energy Program for 1980. 1 am sure many members of this House and Canadians in general have taken the time now to read it. The minister is continually touting it as a great move in terms of Canadianization. I refer all members of this House to page 45 of that document. We find that the purpose of the bill is to:
Ensure active development of oil and gas rights.
At page 47 of "The National Energy Program" we find:
-vigorous and sustained exploration and development efforts should be expected. This has not always been the case-
Further down in the same paragraph we find:
This is no longer appropriate,-*
It continues:
A main feature of the new system, therefore, will be stiffer work requirements,-
In the same paragraph we find:
Other means will include drilling orders, production orders,-
From page 48 we find a little section which I am sure the minister is sending out to environmentalists and those people concerned with the fishing industry around Canada. I quote:
Among the changes will be more rigorous requirements for environmental protection, particularly as regards responsibilities of operators and their absolute liability in case of pollution-causing accidents.
That sounds great. However, it falls apart pretty quickly. It is clear for all to see that the cumulative escape clauses which the energy minister put in this bill make absolute liability unlikely at best. If a billion dollar blowout were to occur off Newfoundland, Melville Island, or off the Queen Charlotte Islands, I can tell Canadians that under this bill as it stands, their recovery for lost fisheries, damaged beaches and so on is not even remotely guaranteed.
What is to stop every drilling rig from becoming individually incorporated? I am sure the minister is abundantly aware of the corporate loopholes which are available to avoid the absolute liability clause and to reduce and fractionally take it down to the point where a billion dollar blowout would in fact be carried on the backs of Canadians and the Canadian environment, and hardly on the backs of those responsible for the spill.
Looking at clause 62(1) of this bill, I note that the Crown is specifically indemnified from almost everything. In fact, I would go further and say the Crown is indemnified from everything, regardless of how or where it occurs.
I point out to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of the Environment, who is in his place, that there are plenty of Mack truck loopholes in this bill. I trust the two of them will see eye to eye long enough to put at least the basic regime for environmental protection into this bill.
There are abundant rumours already that the absolute liability clause will not only, as I already pointed out, get into the fractionalized state but will turn out to be no more than sleight of hand when this bill returns from committee stage. This was one of the very few potential incentives to good
post-exploratory stewardship of the environment. However, the following is revealing.
I pointed out a moment ago a quotation that 1 am sure the Minister of the Environment and the Minister of Energy could send to those people concerned about the environment. Here is one they can send out to the energy industry, just one page further on. I quote:
The new legislation for the Canada lands makes oil and gas rights available for development and hence is not directly concerned with pollution prevention per se.
You cannot have it both ways. You cannot send a little out here and a little out there. I would encourage Canadians to read this bill because it is the greatest jurisdictional grab of the century anywhere in the world. This is an area three times the size of the ten provinces combined. That once again says it all.
The dangers to the Arctic environment were laid out well by my colleague, the hon. member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Ittinuar). This includes areas such as Lancaster Sound where only a tiny fraction of the required scientific work has been done to understand the complex and fragile biological systems of that area. Yet every day there are announcements of nuclear powered icebreakers, LNG tankers three times the size of football fields moving through an area that I remind both ministers is so incredibly fragile that the tiniest mistake could disrupt the biological system and we would end up with little or almost no life in that area which is so crucial.
Where in this lengthy Bill C-48 is the requirement for scientific environmental study and evaluation by independent scientists? It is simply not there. Where is the clause to provide for mandatory public hearings? Gone. The interests of the Inuit, the maritimers, northerners and citizens of British Columbia are not given one paragraph or even one line in this document that I would describe as being greedy.
The people of Canada can take little solace from this document that their interests have been upheld or that the biology and environment of Canada will be protected as they can and must be. Canadians are environmentally conscious, and are sick and tired of corporate Liberal party apologists. This bill is a recipe for get bucks quick, regardless of the costs to the environment and future generations.
I would stress to the two ministers sitting here, avidly reading, that they speak to some of the senior scientists who are well aware of the costs which can be saved by having proper, long-term, broad based environmental studies done. If you disrupt the salmon fishery, you may cost the economy billions more dollars than simply rushing headlong into a rash program trying to grab gas and oil to buoy up a sagging Canadian economy.
The minister touts the 25 per cent Crown share as the outstanding benefit to all Canadians, but under a little pressure in this House on December 11 he admitted to the nymphomaniacs from the oil industry boardrooms to my right that the 25 per cent Crown share is nothing but a hollow promise. He said, as reported at page 5669 of Hansard, that the 25 per cent federal cash incentive grant would be made
January 15, 1981

available to all explorers to offset the 25 per cent Crown share. Here you have it, and there it goes.
What consolation is there in this bill for maritimers for protection of the environment? I can tell everyone in maritime Canada, including maritime British Columbia and the maritime Arctic, that there is absolutely nothing. There is no ownership or protection, just the big Liberal corporate hand ripping off some profit.
What of the offshore in British Columbia, in particular relating to a question which was put to the Minister of the Environment yesterday? He said he knows of no reasons at this point why he should not continue supporting the environmental moratorium. 1 understand that outside of the House he indicated that perhaps the lifting of the moratorium in relation to gas and oil drilling would not affect the tanker traffic.
1 have done enough investigation into this situation to know that there is only one moratorium that was put in place. I have a letter from the Minister of Energy dated September 24, 1980, where he lays out quite clearly that the environmental moratorium was put in place in 1972 during Canada-U.S. negotiations to deal with the risks and liabilities of oil tanker traffic carrying Prudhoe Bay oil down to the continental United States. The moment it was brought in to deal with tanker traffic in Canada-U.S. negotiations, at the very same time it shut down gas and oil exploration. I am sure both ministers know that. 1 am glad to know that the Minister of the Environment at least will stand up for that environmental moratorium to stay in place until there is some reason for it to be lifted. I am sure the House will have the opportunity to debate those reasons when they come forward.
What of the offshore in British Columbia, an area of crucial importance for the production of food, not only salmon, halibut, cod, herring, shellfish and so on, but an area just awakening to the vast potential of marine farming and aquaculture, something we will need not only in Canada but to feed the hungry millions of the world, as pointed out yesterday by my colleague from Saskatoon East during question period?
I challenge any Liberal in this House or any Liberal who will come to this House, and 1 am confident that not one will rise to accept the challenge to put on the record what broad based environmental studies have been done or will be done, studies that deal with the impact of oil drilling or exploration on Pacific salmon and groundfish, studies on the impact of oil and gas blowouts on the estuaries of such massive rivers as the Nass or Skeena, studies on the impact of spills on kelp beds, algae, beaches and so on.
The Minister of the Environment attended the National Survival Institute in Toronto quite recently and listened, as I did, to the chairman of the United Nations environment program where he pointed out the damage being done by toxic and other forms of pollution to the oceans. It is one of the greatest concerns we could possibly have. It is in that final area that we may find the solution to the problem of food for the world and also the production of oxygen to keep us all alive. This sudden, rushed plan is like building a skyscraper
Canada Oil and Gas Act
without ever having an architect or engineer draw up plans or test the ground for stability.

Unbelievable though it may seem, planning can in fact save money, as 1 pointed out to the Minister of Energy. It may take a little more time, but it is extremely important in the strategy of this country. Since the Minister of the Environment is here,
I might point out that it is peculiar that north of 60 in this country the federal government only sees fit to have eight professional biologists doing all of the work related to an area much larger than most countries in this world and far more fragile than the majority of this planet. The rights of fishermen not only in British Columbia but also in the maritimes, and of Inuit fishermen, are eroded in this bill. The rights of coastal residents and native people are beaten back. Every Canadian can wave goodbye to another area of democratic rights if Bill C-48 is passed in its present form.
Let us take a look at who really benefits from Bill C-48 in British Columbia. First and foremost is Chevron. As 1 think the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources knows well, it is in the final stages of having Sea Consult prepare its initial environmental impact. The minister and his officials have indicated to me that shortly after that the environmental moratorium will be lifted so that Chevron can get on with its drilling when the new regime of Bill C-48 is in place. With the passage of the forthcoming new Canada oil and gas act implementing a new regime for Canada Lands, as described in the new National Energy Program which was tabled in the House on October 28, the confidential period for geological and geophysical data will be reduced to five years, or when the lands on which the work was carried out revert to the Crown, whichever is the earlier. The minister also said the following:
Initial steps are now being taken to clear the area for renewed exploratory activity, including drilling, following the undertaking of appropriate environmental studies. Although the results of the 1967-69 drilling campaign by Shell were largely negative, subsequent geological and geophysical studies indicate that the west coast area may have a significant potential for hydrocarbons, particularly gas-
At this point in time I think the minister knows as well as I do-I am sure both ministers know-that touting gas, as Chevron is touting gas, is not really the potential they are interested in finding out about out there. The Geological Survey of Canada in its results released last fall made it quite clear that it expects a one in three chance of 300 million barrels of crude off the B.C. coast and a one in ten chance of perhaps as much as four billion barrels. protected, if it is decided by the public that it is in the public interest to have those drilling programs.

immediate right and by the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans.

Mr. Speaker, it is with great pride that 1 rise once again in this House in order to take part in a debate on a widely discussed bill which, fortunately, has the support of most Canadians. Last October 28, Mr. Speaker, the government tabled its budget and submitted its energy policy the aims of which cannot be reiterated often enough. First, security of supply, and ultimately energy self-sufficiency for Canada; second, the opportunity for all Canadians to be involved in the energy industries, especially the oil and natural gas sector; and, third, fairness in pricing and revenue-sharing between government and industry.
Naturally, Mr. Speaker, energy self-sufficiency for Canada, which is our aim for 1990, combined with a reasonable pricing policy, may only be achieved through considerable government intervention. We must not forget either, Mr. Speaker, that here in Canada multinational corporations operate in privileged conditions compared to what they have to cope with in other countries, and by other countries, Mr. Speaker, I mean

January 15, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
those in which they are still allowed to enter. We all remember, for instance, that just before Christmas Prime Minister Thatcher of Great Britain decided to impose a heavy surtax on all multinationals drilling for oil in the North Sea. But it is south of the border, in the U.S.A., that companies are definitely getting a good deal. The United States policy of deregulating the energy industry is a political scheme which, according to U.S. politicians, corresponds to their specific needs, which are not necessarily the needs of Canadians. To compare our energy policy and wish that it were identical with the American policy is, to my mind, like comparing apples and oranges.
However, Mr. Speaker, this deregulating policy in the United States is certainly very interesting for energy contractors and this is precisely one of the reasons a move to the south is attractive on the very short term. To my mind, Mr. Speaker, that self-sufficiency we want to attain by 1990 would mean nothing if we went from a dependency on the OPEC members to a dependency on multinationals whose boards of directors and shareholders have absolutely no roots in Canada. This is why it is imperative that we should intervene immediately within this industry, in spite of the upheaval that this implies. I am convinced that the Canadian people support an increased participation by government agencies and public corporations in the energy industries, but 1 am also convinced that if there is a shortage one day, the federal government would also be blamed. 1 believe that the Canada oil and gas bill will bring some relief to Canadians because we will have greater independence and security of supply.
Bill C-48, whose second reading was moved on December 11, shows that, as a responsible government, we want to find solutions to the problems of future generations of Canadians since it will allow all Canadian citizens, wherever they live, to share in the wealth of their country. To provide a better understanding of this bill, I would like to point out immediately that it does not affect the territory of the provinces, but only Canada lands. The territory included in the Canada lands is defined as follows in section 2 of the bill:
-lands that belong to Her Majesty in right of Canada, or in respect of which Her Majesty in right of Canada has the right to dispose of or exploit the natural resources, situated in
(a)	the Yukon Territory or the Northwest Territories, or
(b)	those submarine areas adjacent to the coast of Canada and extending throughout the natural prolongation of the land territory of Canada to the outer edge of the continental margin or to a distance of two hundred nautical miles from the baselines from which the breadth of the territorial sea of Canada is measured, whichever is the greater;
Mr. Speaker, as the previous speaker noted, we are speaking about a very vast territory which includes an offshore area of 2.5 million square miles and 1.5 million square miles of land on the continent, which is more than twice the territory of our ten provinces. As the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) said so eloquently, and I quote:
The potential of this vast frontier region is comparable to its size.
Mr. Speaker, all these Canadian territories and the oil fields, which will no doubt be found there, can only enrich
Canada. Mr. Speaker, with this bill, the Canadian people will certainly come out on the winning side.
It is with pride that 1 take part in this most important debate. The new legislation before the House represents one of the most important steps announced in "The National Energy Program" to increase the level of Canadian ownership and control of the petroleum industry to 50 per cent by 1990 on Canada lands. In effect, this legislation represents an affirmation of the government's view that these resources on Canada lands, including offshore resources, belong to all the people of Canada.
I have always tried-and my record speaks for itself-to emphasize that Canadian federalism is and must be based upon the concept of sharing. One of the most important ways to make that concept a reality is to ensure, as this legislation ensures, that all Canadians working through their federal government have the opportunity to participate in the oil and gas industry and thereby share in the benefits of its growth and development. We would be deluding ourselves if we thought for one instant that such sharing would be actualized and such an equilibrium obtained in the absence of direct intervention by our national government.
It is precisely this fact which underlies the 50 per cent ownership requirement with respect to the granting of all new production licences for oil and gas in the Canada lands. Also it is this fact which underlies the 25 per cent interest provision about which I should like to comment in further detail.
By way of review, and so as to refresh the minds of my colleagues opposite, this new Canada oil and gas bill provides that the Crown may carry a 25 per cent share in acreage where production had not started prior to January 1, 1976, in respect of all Canada lands in the offshore and in the territories.

I cannot imagine how one can talk intelligently about this bill and not basically refer to the bill as such; it is simply stupid. 1 have read the bill and I am quoting from it so that members opposite will not put in doubt any of the words 1 am saying, or any of the objectives of the bill. Our objectives are quite clear. We want the industries on the Canada lands to belong to Canadians, not to the multinationals. The multinationals in this country are privileged compared to the way they are treated in other countries.
Similarly if the relevant Crown corporation chooses not to convert the share to a working interest before the specified point in time, the share would return to the Crown and be made available by public tender to Canadians or Canadian companies having a COR of 75 per cent or more.
Much has been said of this 25 per cent interest provision on our new energy program. Indeed, one of the more esteemed members on the opposite side called it "confiscation". Members opposite, as well as certain oil interests, cry that we are expropriating lands which will scare investors away from new development projects. I have received letters, as have many of my colleagues, indicating that we have now changed the rules after the game was played. I disagree with members opposite and I disagree with the multinationals; I do not accept those arguments on the basis of several facts.
First, let us make no pretentions about the poor reception granted our National Energy Program by the private sector. This reaction is understandable, given the fact that the National Energy Program and its various provisions are perhaps against the immediate interests of the multinationals. Of course it is to be expected that oil companies will object to relinquishing a share of their oil interests to the Crown. However, as I have emphasized in all my speeches, our programs and policies must go beyond serving the specific interests of any one sector or region of our economy. For this reason we have attempted to initiate legislation which is fair to the industry, to the federal government, and to all the various provinces and regions of our country.
More specifically, we do not accept the arguments propounded by industry spokesmen and by my colleagues opposite to the effect that any aspect of our National Energy Program-more specifically the legislation concerning the Canada lands-is unfair to the oil industry or is detrimental to its future stability. Central to this position is the assumption that the petroleum industry will lack the needed cash for exploration and development of new sources of supply. Nothing could be further from the truth. In addition to the new pricing schedule increase in producer netbacks per barrel of conventional oil and the provision of a direct cash flow to the industry as a whole, the generous new system of exploration incentives,
Canada Oil and Gas Act
whereby companies will be able to obtain up to 80 per cent of their exploration costs dependent upon their COR, provides ample initiative to the private sector to invest in high risk oil exploration and development ventures. Surely no oil company or investor will lose any capital or the profits it might yield in the face of such extensive government subsidies.
It is true that the 25 per cent share provision in oil projects on the Canada lands being retroactive represents a change in prior policy that may alter the conditions under which some oil exploration projects were begun. But, is this really such an unusual move? Is it not so, each and every time a government announces new restrictions or controls deemed necessary to protect and enhance its national interest, that the conditions or rules upon which investors originally committed their capital will be modified as a matter of course?
As for the corresponding argument that the Crown is unfairly snatching something away from these investors, some such critics seem to have conveniently forgotten that the Crown, on behalf of Canadian citizens, in effect is taking possession of what it has already paid for. That is to say, in the absence of the complex system of tax incentive provisions, oil depletion allowances and so on which were in effect in the past, such exploration might not have begun at all, for, through those tax provisions, the federal treasury and all Canadian taxpayers have paid for approximately 90 per cent of oil exploration and development projects undertaken by the private sector in federal lands. Is it now so unusual for the Crown, as an investor like any other, to demand its due, namely, a reasonable share of the profits?

that Bill S-16, respecting the President of the Lethbridge Stake of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, be read a second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills and Standing Orders.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill S-16 was given third reading by the Senate on December 11, 1980. The purpose of this bill is to grant a new charter to a religious corporation that is responsible for the management and control of the property, affairs and interests in Canada of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, commonly referred to as the Mormon Church.
1 should explain to you at the outset the meaning of the word "stake". A stake is a territorial division of the Mormon Church. As such, it is roughly the equivalent of what would be a diocese in other churches. Within a stake there are generally about ten congregational units known as wards, each of which is headed by a bishop. A ward is roughly the equivalent of a parish as generally understood in other churches.
In 1927, by private act of the Parliament of Canada, namely, chapter 112 of the Statutes of Canada, 1926-27, the President of the Lethbridge Stake was incorporated as a corporation sole. A corporation sole is a corporation consisting of one person only, together with his sucessors in office, who are incorporated by law in order to give them the legal capacities and benefits of a corporation, which they do not enjoy as natural persons. One particular advantage is that of perpetuity.
One of the principal purposes of the corporation sole that is the subject of this bill is to manage and control the property, affairs and interests in Canada of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. The corporation, in addition to managing the affairs of the Church in the Lethbridge area, acts in effect as a holding company for the property and assets of the various missions and stakes of the Church in Canada.
Hon. members may know that the first Mormons in Canada were pioneers who emigrated from Utah in 1887. These pioneers were agricultural settlers and settled in southwestern Alberta. In fact, they have a temple in Cardston, Alberta. The Mormons were responsible for the irrigation of southern Alberta and they began the first sugar beet factory there. The major contribution of irrigation is to food production in Canada.
Since its enactment in 1927, the original act or incorporation of the President of the Lethbridge Stake has never been amended. It contains, for instance, certain limitations on the holding of property that are now archaic and that can only be corrected by Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, 1 wish to proceed with the statement I was making before Christmas, when I was interrupted by the clock. I was quoting among other things part of a working paper tabled at the First Ministers' Conference on the Economy held from the 27th to the 29th of November in Halifax and I was quoting the following statistics on fisheries:
The main species taken throughout the country are: whitefish (6,803.8 metric tons), pickerel (3,855.6 metric tons), great northern pike (2,721.7 metric tons), cisco (1,769 metric tons) . . . Locally, some species such as carp (Saskatchewan and Ontario), arctic char (Northwest Territories), sunfish, smelt, pike, lake perch and eel (Ontario) make up a substantial part of the catches.
The author of the paper then deals with the fishing gear, the accessibility of some lakes, transportation problems, parasites peculiar to some species and the impact of some contaminants, such as mercury, which have led to highly controversial restrictions and have resulted in lower catches of some species.
in addition to stock management, all matters dealing with the protection of the habitat, with processing, transportation and preservation, on which the quality of the product depends, and all marketing related activities have a direct influence on the income and standard of living of freshwater commercial fishermen. Incidentally, at this point I want to mention that according to the 1978 report, in 1972 most freshwater fishermen earned $3,700 and the average annual income was $5,900 whereas the national average in the fishing industry was $6,900 annually. The fact was stressed that, in central Canada, fishing was mainly a part time occupation and in the higher income brackets, only half was derived from fishing.

For all those reasons, in 1965 the federal government asked Mr. George Mclvor by order in council to look into the matter and report on the situation of freshwater fishermen in the provinces of Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, as well as in the Northwest Territories, with special emphasis on product marketing. The resulting report, the Mclvor commission report, led to the setting up, on February 27, 1969, of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation.
The corporation, created by the Freshwater Fish Marketing Act of 1969, was established for the purpose of marketing and trading fish, fish products and fish byproducts in and out of Canada, to ensure the most rational marketing at every level of the industry, and the best and most stable prices possible for the fishermen's catches.
Initial costs in setting up the corporation were subsidized, but it is now financially self-sufficient and does not receive any financial assistance from Parliament. The corporation is financed through bank loans guaranteed by the Minister of Finance or even direct loans. It consists of a board of directors composed of a chairman, a president, one director for each of the participating provinces and four other directors each of whom is to be appointed by the governor in council for a term not exceeding five years. The corporation is accountable to Parliament through the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. By its very nature and because of its terms of reference the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation is an easy target for complaints.
Let us be fair. The corporation does not have but one customer, it has 3,500 of them in the sense that, in a position of monopoly, it serves some 3,500 fishermen spread out over a vast area consisting of four provinces and the Northwest Territories and which are as many partners whose interests are quite strongly differentiated. The corporation must buy all fish caught in fresh water by commercial fishermen, a task
January 15, 1981

which it accomplishes directly or indirectly through designated agents.
The corporation sets an initial price to be paid to the fishermen. It sees to it that the fish is processed, packed and sold either on the domestic market or abroad, mostly in the United States which buys 90 per cent of our catches. It later pays a refund to fishermen as a final payment. Assuming everything proceeds in a normal way, it would be a miracle if all those involved in such complex dealings, on their own admission, were to be totally satisfied.
Therefore it was no surprise, on December 4, 1979, following a meeting between the federal Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and his counterparts of the provinces and territories involved, to learn that they had looked into the role played by the corporation and wanted it defined for the future, and that a federal-provincial committee of officials was given the task of preparing an in-depth analysis of the processing and marketing activities of the corporation, as well as its administrative, financial and operational structures. The interested partners were to be informed of the results of such a study at a meeting to be held in Winnipeg before the end of April last.
The April, 1980, meeting was never held. On the one hand, the study was pursued and, on the other hand, there was an election and the former government, which had commissioned the study, experienced certain problems. The study was finally completed and the report, we are informed, was recently tabled. What more can we ask? That we undertake a further study over the head of the committee which was set up for the very purpose? Personally, I do not see the need for it and I am sure hon. members agree with me on that point. The press release of December 4, 1979, which was over a year ago, stated, and I quote:
In the meantime, the cabinet ministers unanimously recommended that the corporation pursue its activities as usual until the findings of the Winnipeg meeting are known.
But the Winnipeg meeting, for reasons that we already know, never took place. Since then, the report was tabled and it is there for all to read. Therefore, unless there are new issues of which we are not aware, 1 do not see why we should force hon. members to consider correspondence between interested parties relating to a matter which, to all intents and purposes, concerns only one department and the corporation it is responsible for.
Mr. Speaker, all that has been said until now leads me to think that some undoubtedly well-meaning people wanted and still want to broaden the social role of the corporation. To be quite frank, it appears some would want to turn it into a social development agency. I shall reserve judgment on that proposal and on the purposes of those who hold that view. 1 think that the issue before the House today does not go that far; it concerns essentially the current role of the corporation which is that of a sales and marketing agency.
