speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation was first formed in 1969 at the request of the provinces involved, the objectives of the new body were quite clear and straightforward; first, to market fish in an orderly manner; second, to promote international markets and increase interprovincial and export trade in fish; and, third and most important, to increase returns to the fishermen in that one and a half million square mile territory. That was a formidable task and, 1 might say, it was generally achieved.
The first objective was met. The corporation has been able to market fish in an orderly manner by investing in capital assets such as fish packing stations and filleting, scaling, grading and freezing equipment so that the fish can be held until the best market is found for it.
On the second objective, international markets have been created. In the early years, some 80 per cent of the fish was sold in the United States. That percentage is now 61 per cent with some 23 per cent going to the European markets and 16 per cent to the Canadian market.
The third objective, and this is the most important, is the returns to fishermen. Before the corporation was formed, the freshwater fishermen were pretty well at the mercy of the buyers. They could not speak as one voice as they do now, and were compelled to accept what the companies were willing to offer them for their hard work. Frankly, it was pretty meagre at times. That situation has changed.
Before Christmas the corporation sent out the largest payments in its 11-year history to the fishermen under its jurisdiction, final payments for the year 1980 that total $5.7 million shared among 3,500 fishermen from the prairie provinces, northwestern Ontario and the Northwest Territories. Those payments are a far cry from the small and unpredictable amounts they received for their fish prior to the establishment of the corporation.
These latest payments are only part of what has been received by the freshwater fishermen this year. If we compare the figures, we find that the figure for 1975-76 was $10 million. In 1976-77 it was $14 million. In 1977-78 it was $15.3 million. In 1978-79 it was $17.2 million. Then there was a phenomenal rise, to $25.5 million in 1979-80.

January 15, 1981
Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation
1 think those are impressive figures. They mean that the corporation is doing its job and is ensuring fishermen steady incomes.
The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) has asked why the report was not tabled sooner. 1 can tell him that it required a longer time to prepare than had first been expected. I may also say that there are no fundamental changes recommended and no requests from the provincial ministers for a meeting with them, and I remind this House that this is an area of the fisheries which is under the management of provincial governments. Certainly if a request were made for a meeting, 1 would be happy to accept.
Now that the corporation is successfully carrying out its mandate, there are members of the opposition who say there are many faults with its operations. How can they come to such a conclusion in the face of such a success story and still claim that it is not a good operation? Frankly, I simply ask them to look at the evidence.
It has already been pointed out that the report of the review committee of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation has now been tabled in this House. The general conclusion of this review committee, composed of provincial and territorial government representatives as well as representatives of the fishermen themselves, is that the fishermen are better off with the existence of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation than without it. The report contains several recommendations to improve the operation of the corporation, and I am informed that some of these recommendations are already being implemented.
i tried to get the hon. member to narrow the request he made for the production of papers. He did not accept my suggestion, and I regret that because the reality is that other than the normal confidential documents which are exchanged between governments-and I would have been ready to approach the provincial governments if a more precise list of documents requested had been submitted to me-I am fully in favour of full information being given to this House or to the general public. The fact remains, however, that because of the broad definition and because of the back dating of the documents which were requested by the hon. member to such an extent, 1 find myself in the position of having to ask the House to reject the motion of the hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, in presenting this motion to the House early in the present session my objective was to request of the minister a sharing with this House of a variety of concerns of which he is well aware, which have been made known to his ministry since the beginning of 1978. In fact the request for production of papers was to go back only as far as January 1, 1978, so I am rather surprised that the minister should suggest that we wanted to go back a great distance in time.
The purpose of the motion was to help bring before this House the sentiments which were expressed, and indeed are still being expressed, by some of the provincial governments
and the territorial councils-most especially the territorial councils in recent weeks-pointing out a number of faults and anomalies which have crept into the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation which have led it to become something quite different from what was initially envisaged.
The FFMC is no longer a marketing board as originally envisaged. It is a vertically integrated monopoly. It is not democratic socialism, which involves private and public sector competition. It is much more pervasive than that in the manner in which it has destroyed community industries and particularly the community lakeside fishing industries of northern Manitoba, Saskatchewan and the Northwest Territories. It has virtually destroyed Co-operative Fisheries Limited, a socialist co-operative in Saskatchewan which operated successfully for many years. It has bankrupted many buyers and processors of fish over the past decade.
Fishermen no longer have a yardstick of comparison in order to know whether the corporation and its chairman, who goes flitting around the world securing buys and deals-and the chairman should not be doing that at all-are getting an adequate price for fishermen. There is a history of sleight of hand in the management and the announcements of the economic state of the corporation. There is the question of payments to fishermen which have been adjusted by docking the transportation charges first in order to create the illusion that the payments to fishermen were 60 per cent of the gross return on fish when in fact they were only 50 per cent. There is the question of $10 million worth of loans. Who knows how much additional deficit has been incurred to allow those higher payments to fishermen this year, of which the minister and his chairman are so proud?
Has anything improved? I have here a copy of the Hay River newspaper dated December 3, 1980, which says "Fishermen pay for FFMC loss". At this very moment this winter the fishermen of the Northwest Territories are being docked an additional eight cents a pound from their final payment, an additional eight cents which the territorial government feels it has no obligation to pay, yet the chairman of the corporation is going around the western provinces bragging about the fact that the final payments are much increased this year and that all the fishermen are doing better.
What about the native fishermen of the Northwest Territories and of the western Arctic? My hon. colleague to my right knows full well the implications of this corporation, some of the questions of mismanagement and the impact these have upon the people he represents.
There was a number of positive recommendations in the report filed by the committee of officials. The next stage would have been to reconvene a meeting of first ministers and to act on those recommendations to which the minister has referred.
I will read one final sentence from the general conclusion of the report, as follows:
However, several modifications to the present marketing system appear to have merit in that they could generate new revenue to the industry without decreasing fishermen's incomes, or, in some cases, by increasing fishermen's incomes.
January 15, 1981

That suggests a recommendation for action, and 1 can only ask at this stage what action the minister plans to take next. I urge him to meet with the first ministers.
With that said, I hereby move that the question be put.

Mr. Speaker, in dealing with Bill C-48 I should now like to refer to some of the clauses to show that the allegation made at the beginning of my remarks that this is a gigantic grab for power can be confirmed in the clauses of the bill.
One clause in the bill states that the bill would permit the minister or his nominee to enter into exploration agreements without prior public notice where he does not consider it to be in the public interest to give such notice. A bill which provides such power to a minister is a dangerous bill. Under this bill ministers are given power to enter into exploration agreements without even giving prior public notice. That is not the democratic way of carrying on business and it is not the way in which business has been carried out for many years in Canada. The public is notified before the minister enters into agreements with anyone, and in the case of contracts everyone is given an equal chance. That is the way it should be.
Again the bill states that while the Crown share of 25 per cent interest does not require the Crown corporation holding the share to pay its proportional share of the exploration and development costs, the Crown corporation will have a full 25 per cent vote in all decisions of the operating committee. Why should Petro-Canada have special privileges? Surely it can stand on its own feet. In a democratic society, particularly a free enterprise society, a Crown corporation should compete with the other companies and not have a monopoly, because a government monopoly is no better than any other kind of monopoly. It is just as dangerous and it does the very same thing. So we are going to give special consideration to this Crown corporation. This discourages private industry and thus drives money out of the country. In a free competitive society people go where they have an equal chance to bid.
In clause 44 it is stated that the minister can declare that a significant discovery has been made and can then order the drilling of additional wells wherever he wants by any party under whose lands the discovery may extend. Surely if a company has spent several million dollars, and that is not unusual, and then makes a discovery, the minister can simply ask up to a maximum of three others to drill. Why is there not a proper plan so that when someone makes a discovery, they will know what to expect? The industries came into Alberta to search for oil because they knew they would get a fair deal. They knew what they would have and what they would not if they made a discovery. Those matters should all be laid down before the people invest their money. It is a logical and sensible way to do it. When people came to Alberta to invest their money, they knew the result might be a dry hole, but if they made a discovery, as was the case in Leduc, Redwater and Mildred Lake, they knew a certain portion of it would be available for others to bid on so that anyone, including them, would have a chance to bid and the highest bidder would get the particular land. They knew what was what.

January 15, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
One of the reasons for the Heritage Fund existing in the province of Alberta is that Alberta has been fair with industry. Because the industry knew that the government would be fair, they were willing to bid thousands and sometimes millions of dollars for some of the areas which had been proven to have oil or gas. Surely that is a sensible way to do it, rather than simply telling them in the act that if they make a significant discovery the minister can create a Crown corporation to take the rest of it or give it to other people. The minister may do it without bidding or purchasing the rights.
Why does the government want such power? Why is it not done above the table or out in the open so that industry knows what is going on? The minister can declare that a commercial discovery has been made and order the drilling of additional wells at the time and place of his choosing without limit on the number of such wells. A typical offshore well could cost $25 million to $50 million. Will the minister order the drilling of additional wells? Will the minister tell a company to drill one or two more wells at a cost of another $50 million? Why is it not done by open bid or giving companies an opportunity to bid? The money will come into the public treasury that way. In fact, millions of dollars came into the Alberta treasury from companies prepared to take a risk because of the chance to make a profit. They were willing to do the work and make a profit. They have done that, and there is nothing wrong with profit.
What are the penalties under the act if a company indicates it cannot drill? Well, let me outline the penalties for non-compliance with the act. It can be fined up to $1 million or imprisoned up to five years for each day on which the offence is committed. Why are those penalties included for someone who does not or cannot obey the direction of the minister?
Surely there should be some freedom of choice in the country. We are not living in Moscow, Russia. We are not under a communist regime. Why have they included this type of communistic legislation? That is what it is; that is what it is. When the minister orders a company to drill and it refuses to drill, it can be fined $1 million or be subjected to imprisonment up to five years. What kind of a country are they developing?
Under clause 59 any corporate officer who acquiesces to the offence is liable. Without going into any more clauses of the bill, I want to ask why any minister should have such power. Why do the backbenchers, particularly on the government side of the House, want the minister to have such power? Why are these things not done above the table by open bid so that everyone will know what is going on? The money would come into the treasury; the highest bidder could go out under government legislation.
I have only one or two other matters I should like to raise because I would like to leave some time for other members. This is a fight with one section of the industry, the multinationals. I have no particular love for the large companies, but they have done a job in this country. They came in and risked their money. Do hon. members opposite know the number of
dry holes? 1 hear hon. members opposite laughing; I would like to see them invest some of their money when there is only a slight chance of finding oil or gas. The large companies risked millions of dollars. They spent millions of dollars before they even found anything. In fact, there are hundreds of dry holes. It is okay to sit back and laugh now that they have spent their money and have proven up wells, and then like some communistic government say, "We will take it over now that they have been found." That is not the kind of country Canadians want.
We should not forget that hundreds of good Canadians are working for these multinational companies. The multinationals can stand anything the government can do; they have the money to withstand anything. But, what about the small Canadian companies? I know the minister received a letter from a small Canadian company because I have a copy of it in my possession. As a matter of fact he received several letters which he did not read when he gave his speech; he read the other ones. Small Canadian companies are being forced to cut back; they just cannot keep up. The minister said there is not one unemployed person. He does not read his mail because that one letter indicated that 19 people were let go. There will be more let go if the government continues its ridiculous and nonsensical policy.

What we need in this country is a climate in which the people can have confidence in their government, where they can invest in equity capital, where they can get out and work, develop this country and be able to make a profit. Mr. Speaker, my contribution this evening will be short, since some 26 speakers have already spoken on this bill. This bill saw the light of day over a month ago and its predecessor. Bill C-20, saw the light of day about three years ago. Therefore, it seems to me it is time for this proposal to proceed to committee as quickly as possible.
What this bill does has been described by many already. I will limit myself and describe five areas in a very brief manner. The first one has to do with the fact that under this proposal the Crown will have an interest position of at least 25 per cent in all Canada lands, including all existing and future grants to be made.
The second thrust of this bill is that it will provide for a minimum acceptable level of Canadian ownership in frontier Canada oil and gas resources to be 50 per cent, with a
Canada Oil and Gas Act
provision in case of deficiency to be reserved by the Crown. That is in the name of the Canadian public.
The next major direction of this bill has to do with the fact that a Crown corporation will have the right to demand from relevant operators geological, well or other proprietary information.
The fourth area has to do with the revolving fund provisions for regional environmental studies by assessing holders of rights in proportion to their acreage holdings. I will return to this measure in light of the remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton).
The fifth area I would like to describe, which the preceding speaker made reference to at great length, is that there are many provisions in this bill for ministerial discretion. I support this. One area of ministerial discretion has to do with the authority given to the minister to prohibit the proposed transfer or assignment of interests on grounds of public interest, therefore, in the name of Canadians.
The question which comes to mind after having looked at the major points contained in this bill is: Where will this legislation apply? It will apply to all the so-called Canada lands, which to me is a new term, and a very interesting one. It includes all the lands in the territories and the offshore, which together total an area of almost 2Vi million square miles in the offshore and about a million and a half square miles in the Yukon and Northwest Territories. 1 find those figures staggering. They total an area of almost twice as large as that of the ten provinces combined. This vast area will represent Canada's best prospects for large new reserves of conventional petroleum.
Let us look for a moment at what Bill C-48 really represents. 1 do not think we should look at it in isolation. 1 submit to you it represents another step on the road initiated many years ago when Parliament approved the National Energy Board Act, when Parliament established the Panarctic, approved the Petro-Canada Act, I believe in 1975 when it approved the Petroleum Administration Act and the Petroleum Corporations Monitoring Act. What we see here is a series of desirable steps stretched over a number of years to develop a situation whereby, in Canada, the public sector will be put into a position to compete and co-operate with the private sector. That will be a good balance when established in the long run. We cannot yet say we have achieved this balance. To those in this debate who have said this bill provides for confiscation, we say that about $3 billion of the taxpayers money, in the form of deferred tax write-offs, have already been made available to the private sector in the oil and gas industry.
In addition, what this bill will do once enacted is give Canadians, by means of the 25 per cent public share I mentioned earlier, something which was very well expressed by the parliamentary secretary to the minister in the debate on December 17. I quote his remarks from page 5868 of Hansard-. "the 25 per cent Crown share is in fact a long overdue catchup for the Canadian people." 1 could not think of a more fitting and effective description of what this 25 per cent public share really means. I am surprised to see why members

opposite, like the member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), cannot see the importance of this measure and what it really represents when put into historical terms. Contrary to what some have said in this debate so far, while this legislation will geographically apply in the north and the offshore, its impact will be felt in the boardrooms of western Canada and eastern Canada. It will be felt in Calgary, yes, but in Toronto, too, by Imperial, Gulf, Texaco, Shell and Suncor. It will be felt in the boardrooms of Montreal as well, at Petrofina and BP. Let us once and for all put to rest this red herring of an east-west confrontation. It is not fair, it is not right, it is not there. It will affect the whole nation in a variety of ways. It certainly is not to be interpreted as one which fires and fuels the tensions that already exist.
What is left here for me is to look at the position taken by the opposition parties. Since this debate started on December 11, inevitably one must have a look at what has been said. Let us start with the position of the Conservative party. On December 11, 1980, the member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) on page 5671 of Hansard is reported as having said:
The broad objectives of this legislation are worthwhile and are certainly acceptable. One might go so far as to say they are motherhood; they are intended to increase production and Canadian ownership, as well as to provide a very stable tax environment.
I wonder how this sounds to the hon. member for Bow River. The hon. member went on to say:
I agree with the minister when he says that it is important to have this legislation. We have been waiting for it for about ten years now.
But this afternoon, as we all heard, the hon. member for Bow River spoke violently in opposition to this bill. We just heard him comparing us to a communist dictatorship. How does he square that with the statement made by the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre. The hon. member for Bow River in his outrage-and I do not know whether it was synthetic or spontaneous-in effect has indicated that the Tories are divided among themselves. The only conclusion which we on this side can draw is that it is business as usual as far as the Progressive Conservative Party is concerned. But when the hon. member for Bow River says he is strenuously opposed to this bill because it gives the government the power to set prices, 1 would invite him to tell us which government in the world today does not set prices for oil and gas.
When the hon. member rejects strenuously the notion of government intervention and says it is a very bad practice, he forgets, and I am sure since he comes from Alberta that it is inadvertent, the Alberta industry was saved in the 1960s by virtue of the Borden line, an initiative which was taken by the Government of Canada. If I remember correctly, it was taken by the second former leader of the hon. member's own party. It would be fair to conclude that all of the 100 Tory members of Parliament, minus one, seem violently opposed to this bill. They say it is bad and that it goes too far. I feel comfortable when they say so because I know then that we are on the right track.
Let us look at the NDP for a moment. The NDP says something that is rather curious. They are opposed to the bill and at page 5676 of Hansard we find this general reasoning flowing from the lips of their guru on natural resources, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), who said:
Suddenly the minister proposes a new program of Canadianization. Essentially this is why we oppose the bill.
His reasoning as outlined in his speech seems to flow along three main lines: (1) suspicion of the government; (2) by saying that the legislation does not go far enough; and (3) accusing the government of claiming it is doing something progressive when there is really no change. I could not help but conclude upon reading the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway that his logic is inspired by the rather peculiar principle that no loaf is better than half. That seems to be the inspiration and guiding principle of the NDP in its approach to this bill.
How is it that on the one hand the NDP can say there is nothing in this bill and, on the other hand, the Tories get upset and say that there is too much in it. I am at a loss to understand their attitudes. Are we witnessing here a case of mass psychology where 100 Tories, minus one, think one way and the NDP thinks diametrically opposite? It seems that is a classic case of an urgent need for group therapy for these politicians because there is no other explanation. For one group the legislation is so bad and for the other there is nothing in the legislation, but they both come to the same conclusion, that they will oppose the bill. The NDP oppose the legislation because their logic is that it is better to have no loaf than to have half a loaf.
In conclusion, 1 express my regret over the speech made this afternoon by the hon. member for Skeena, for whom I have the highest respect. The hon. member who is the NDP saint for the environment spoke this afternoon from an environmental point of view. If I heard him correctly he described the bill as an absolute zero. He went on to challenge any Liberal backbencher in this House to show that this bill makes provision for environmental studies. The bill in fact does make provision for environmental studies. Section 49, from page 27 to page 29, of the bill is devoted to such studies. It spells out in detail how and by whom an environmental studies fund is to be established and administered, including 11 subclauses with one subclause on regulations and one subclause indicating the fund is not to exceed $15 million. Instead of making silly challenges, the NDP critic might take the time to read this bill and do his homework.
We on this side of the House take a position which is between the Conservatives and the NDP. We think this bill is another important step forward in Canada's history. Whenever one goes outside the borders of this country today he learns that there is not a person who does not speak with envy of Canada and describes it as the world envy because of its natural resources. Generations of Canadians in this and the next century will benefit from the implementation of the ideas contained in the bill; of that I am absolutely certain. In the
January 15, 1981

same way we now say it was a good idea to create Panarctic some 15 years ago; in the year 2000 they will say it is a good idea that we pushed ahead with Bill C-48, for the benefit of generations of Canadians, with its principles of public ownership Canadianization, and strong powers in the capital of the nation in the interest of the full community from coast to coast, from east to west and from north to south.
It is too bad the NDP does not have the guts to support the bill, and it is too bad the Tories once again, as at the time of the bill establishing Petro-Canada, have to be dragged so recalcitrancy into the twentieth century.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member expressed concern about our stand on this bill. As he is aware, the bill seeks to obtain legal control in right of Her Majesty the Queen of the resources off the east coast of Canada which go out 200 miles. I am sure he is aware that in 1621 King James I granted the Royal Charter of Nova Scotia to Sir William Alexander. In recognition of the utter dependence of the early colonists on the sea for food and transportation, the King included as part of our territory a band of sea stretching about 120 miles southward from our coast. That band easily covers the area which is known as Sable Island and it covers part of Georges Bank as well as most of the Scotian shelf. I should like to ask the hon. member how this government can legally, in the name of Her Majesty, the Queen, take away from us as Nova Scotians, this territory which was granted to us by the King in the year 1621 ?

Mr. Speaker, I believe this is the first time, and it is certainly the first time in my memory, we have concurrently before Parliament two government measures that are operating under the invocation of closure, under the rule of Standing Order 75c.
I refer, of course, to the government's constitutional package as contained in the joint resolution now before the joint committee of the House and Senate. We know that the parliamentary guillotine will fall on that committee on February 6, even though we have just commenced clause by clause study of the 59 clauses. We started on clause 1 yesterday. We know that under the order the House invoked by closure, that measure has to be reported back to the House and to the Senate on or before February 6.
When that measure was going through the House the point was made repeatedly, especially by those of us who had the opportunity to participate-and indeed, it was made dramati-
Canada Oil and Gas Act
cally by those who were denied the opportunity to participate-that the constitutional package was probably one of the most important bills to come before Parliament. We said that in the context of putting forward arguments on why the time for debate on that important measure should be extended.
It is interesting that Bill C-48, which is now before us, has had closure invoked on it at this stage. We know that the parliamentary guillotine under rule 75c will come down on second reading of this bill in less than an hour.
I heard the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), for whom I have great respect, and I am sorry he is not in the House at the moment but I understand he had to leave, participate in the debate a few moments ago. Some members may ask what is wrong with that. On the face of it there is nothing wrong, except when it is remembered that the hon. member for Davenport also participated in the debate last night which invoked closure on this bill. Indeed, I believe he was the last member to speak on the closure motion, putting forward arguments of why it should be invoked.
It would seem logical and fair to me that if he were to speak in support of a motion to invoke closure, a measure that would limit severely the time left to debate this important measure- a measure, I submit, almost as important as the one now before the committee in terms of its impact on the country- he should not then deprive somebody else of the precious right to speak in the few hours we have left by virtue of the invocation of closure, notwithstanding how important the message the hon. member felt he had to deliver in the debate.
I would say to the hon. member for Davenport that in a parliamentary sense that just is not fair. He is responsible for closure. He has to assume his collective share of responsibility for closure. By speaking tonight he deprived another hon. member who opposed the imposition of closure of the right to speak.
This bill brings a new element into the constitutional debate in terms of the Canada lands. It is that feature of the bill I want to address for a few moments this evening.
It is well to recall that the issue of resource ownership which is now a question seized by the constitutional committee and the debate surrounding the constitution in the country, was raised during the First Ministers' conference, particularly with regard to the offshore dimensions of that resource question. It has been raised in the House in the form of questions. It has been raised because the province of Newfoundland and the province of Nova Scotia have put forward claims to the ownership of the offshore. We have been told by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the House that this is a question for the Supreme Court of Canada to decide. If the federal government claims ownership and if the provinces claim ownership, then I submit it is not unreasonable for the Prime Minister and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to suggest that this matter should be settled by a third party, namely, the Supreme Court of Canada.

They also said during the meeting of first ministers that the package on the table, and presumably the package we are dealing with tonight in the constitutional committee, was merely the first phase of the government's constitutional proposals, and that the resource question would be included in the second phase.
Here we have two positions: one taken in the House by the government saying that the question of who has claim to the offshore is to be settled by the court and another position taken at the First Ministers' conference by the same government saying that the question of the offshore and the resource question will come in the second phase of the ongoing constitutional package.
What I find strange is that we now have this bill before us which will get second reading tonight by the use of the government's majority which makes a complete mockery of any suggestion that this matter should be included in the second phase of constitutional discussions or that it should be settled by the Supreme Court of Canada.
The bill assumes that the legal ownership of the Canada lands in the maritime provinces and Newfoundland belongs to the federal jurisdiction of Canada. That seems to me to fly in the face of what we have been told in this House and to fly in the face of the constitutional process that started this summer in which the first ministers were told that it was to be the second phase of the government's constitutional process.
Is the government now saying to the premiers who attended that conference in September that it has taken the offshore question off the list? Is that what it is saying by this bill? Is that the message going to the Atlantic provinces tonight? Or is the federal government telling the House and the Canadian people that there will be no second phase to the constitutional process, that the phase we have now is the final and irrevocable process.
On the one hand the federal government admits that the ownership of the offshore resources is a question for the Supreme Court of Canada, and now the government is asking Parliament to pass an act to give the rights of the offshore to the federal government.
I am not a lawyer, sir, but it would seem to me that given the due process in this country and the separation of the judicial process from the parliamentary process, the government would have waited until this matter was settled by the court. That is what we would expect and that is what the provinces had every right to expect.
Bill C-48 assumes that all the offshore area off the east coast of Canada is Canada lands owned by the Government of Canada for the people of Canada. My friend from South Shore (Mr. Crouse) put forward an argument on behalf of his province. My province has put forward another argument. I suppose this will have to be ultimately decided by the courts, the passage of this bill notwithstanding. But what that does to
the process, I do not know. My province makes the case, and rightly so, and I have made it in this House, that we brought with us into the federation, into the union, our jurisdiction intact over the offshore lands, which is the continental shelf.
The government disputes that, and that is its right. 1 say that dispute should not be on the floor of this House in the form of a bill put through by the invocation of closure with the use of the majority. That should be settled by due process before the Supreme Court of Canada.
It assumes considerable importance for some of us because we are dealing interestingly with what the bill calls Canada lands. That means, of course, land under the sea on the continental shelf. We should take a look at what has happened to Canada land in the past. Prior to the Canada we now know there were lands which were Canada lands. We know, for example, that as a result the face of Canada has changed, not only with the creation of new provinces, but with the expansion by the federal government of the existing boundaries of existing provinces. I might say this has had the effect of placing the Atlantic provinces, by this bill, at an all time disadvantage because the only place we can expand our lands is by the lands which the government is now claiming in this bill.
It is well for us to remember what the Government of Canada did in extending the boundaries and what it meant for Quebec. It meant an addition of 379,000 square miles to the territory of Quebec in 1912, without which the province could not have the tremendous James Bay hydro development and all the vast energy that will mean for the province and people of Quebec.
The province of Ontario had its boundary extended by
237,000	square miles to the north and to the west to what is now the boundary of Manitoba. We have seen the boundary of Saskatchewan and Alberta each given an additional 250,000 square miles which were northern lands-Canada lands- under the jurisdiction of Canada and belonging to all Canadians.
Simple justice would indicate that the only boundaries of our region to be extended are those on the continental shelf. That is a natural extension of our land mass. The continental shelf is recognized by international law as the natural extension of a land mass of a coastal state. That simple justice is being denied to us by this government. We know. There is a good reason for it.
Off our own coast, Hibernia basin has a potential of 1 billion barrels of recoverable oil. It is there in commercial quantities. Unfortunately, I am sorry to say, the development of it is being held up because of this dispute. It is not being helped, I might add, by the passage of this kind of legislation. We know there is natural gas and probably oil reserves off the coast of Nova Scotia. The natural gas is there. Whether or not the oil is there in recoverable quantities has yet to be determined, but it is probably there. We know there is natural gas in commercial quantities off the coast of Labrador, all of which is included in the Canada lands in the bill now before us.
January 15, 1981

Coming from a province with only 53.6 per cent of the earned income of the average Canadian and with unemployment insurance in terms of our economy representing one-twelfth of the personal income in Newfoundland as compared to one-fortieth in the rest of Canada, we are being denied the right by this kind of legislation to be able to stand on our own feet economically as a result of what that tremendous oil resource would mean to us. That does not mean the Government of Newfoundland wants to grab it all and keep it all. The government of Newfoundland has made the case as to why it is so concerned with exercising its claim. First it wants to control the rate of development. That is very important to an old culture like ours. We know what has happened in other jurisdictions. We have a precious fishery resource, not only a social resource in terms of our people and our way of life, but we have a fishery resource on which that social resource depends. We must protect that and hence control the rate of development. The only way we can control the rate of development is if we control the resource. Let no one think that we claim that because we want all of it to ourselves. We are prepared to share with the rest of Canada. The Government of Canada will get its share from its tax powers. The developer will get its share from its royalties and Newfoundland will get its share. From our share we will be able to contribute in terms of the equalization formula to the rest of Canada. Is it wrong or is it fair that we should look for our place in the sun by something which we feel is justifiably and rightfully ours?
1 was proud when we sat on that side, albeit for a short time. We had a policy in place which provided that the province of Newfoundland would own the mineral resources of the continental shelf. The ownership and legislative jurisdiction would be consistent with and subject to the division of legislative competence as between Parliament and the provincial legislatures under the Constitution of Canada; that the Government of Canada would continue to have legislative jurisdiction in certain areas such as environment, shipping, and so on. Those principles would be confirmed by the signing of an agreement which we agreed to enter into between the two governments and by appropriate legislative action and constitutional change. All that stopped with the change in government last year.
I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that the passage of this bill with the government claiming upon itself these Canada lands and so denying the right of the Atlantic provinces to extend in the only way they can is an act of grave injustice to the people of Atlantic Canada and one which hon. members opposite will have to account for when they face the people.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph Ferguson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State, Small Businesses):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-48, an act to regulate the oil and gas interests in Canada lands and to amend the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act, is an act designed specifically to safeguard the interests of the people of Canada and their energy resources on our Canadian-owned lands, sometimes referred to as Crown land. In simple
Canada OH and Gas Act
terms, these are lands owned by Canada as a nation or Canadians collectively and we all have an interest in the development of those lands and the resources on those lands.
I want to stress that this act does not in any way infringe upon the rights or ownership of mineral rights of the provinces, but in the interpretation of the bill, Canada lands are defined as lands that belong to Her Majesty in the right of Canada or with respect to which Her Majesty in the right of Canada has the right to dispose of or exploit the natural resources. It is for this reason I indicated earlier that we as individual Canadians have a vital interest that must be safeguarded for our future generations. It is intended to ensure Canada's energy resources for the eighties and to upgrade and update existing legislation currently applied to these lands.
In simple terms, its intent is to ensure that the 300 million acres of land currently under lease in these regions is developed, bearing in mind the best interests of Canada and of Canadians and, in particular, ensuring that Canadian-owned companies are involved in the development and accrue the benefits from this development. I believe, however, before we go into the specifics of this legislation, in this debate on second reading, we should recap or compare in a very brief way similar legislation and regulation and returns to other companies in other nations.
Oil companies would lead us to believe that we in Canada are asking too much, but in England there is one state-owned company empowered to purchase 51 per cent of all oil production, and another one with a monopoly on gas production. In Norway, a Norwegian state enterprise established since 1973 is empowered to carry a 50 per cent interest in oil and gas rights in the exploration stage, and that rate can go as high as 80 per cent. Similar stringent state involvement also exists in Indonesia.
Mexico completely nationalized its oil industry many years ago, from the exploration and development stage, through processing, distributing and retail sales.
Venezuela has taken similar measures and, although several multinationals had been extensively involved in the Venezuelan petroleum industry, the industry is now totally nationalized under PetroVen and four subsidiary companies. But these four subsidiaries work very closely with the multinationals such as Exxon.
In the Middle East, in Saudi Arabia there are two state-owned companies, Iranco and PetroMin, and again these companies are working in the interests of the country and in co-operation with the multinationals. This same situation exists throughout the Middle East and it is worthy of note that the multinationals now handle less than 50 per cent of world trade. If the multinationals are willing to work closely with state-owned companies in other countries, under far more rigid controls and rules than we propose, why can they not work with Canadians in Canada?
It is not our intention to nationalize the oil industry. We have only one Petro-Canada at the present time. Some

January 15, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
Canadians and members of this House would lead us to believe that the National Energy Policy is creating undue hardships on the multinationals operating in Canada, but when you compare the stricter controls and lower allowable involvement imposed in other countries, naturally they will complain. A negative reaction was to be expected here in Canada as we Canadianize our industry, through a more direct involvement of Petro-Canada and the involvement of Canadians investing in and securing our energy supplies for the years ahead.
One other interesting aspect of the energy policies of these other countries is the fact that very few of them charge world prices to their own consumers. In other words, they charge world prices for their exported oil and another price for oil and gas used for domestic consumption. Some of the comparisons are as follows: in Mexico gasoline is 20 cents per litre, in Venezuela 4.4 cents per litre, in Saudi Arabia 5.5 cents per litre, England 76.2 cents a litre, Canada 31 cents per litre, the United States 37 cents a litre, in France 90 cents per litre and Italy 100.08 cents per litre. This is all quoted in Canadian dollars.
This act is intended to replace the Territorial Lands Act, and Public Lands Act and includes amendments to the Oil and Crown Production and Conservation Act. But the basic objective is to provide security of supply for Canadians and to provide the vehicle for Canadian participation in energy development and revenue sharing.
At the same time, we intend to pursue the development of frontier oil and gas, while ensuring that Canadians receive a fair return for these oil and gas resources, optimizing the employment of Canadians and the use of Canadian goods and services in frontier gas and oil exploration and development.
Our proposed legislation and the National Energy Policy is the best in the world. It respects the needs of the oil companies and protects the heritage and interests of Canadians.
To those members who would suggest that a 25 per cent share in oil and gas rights for Canadians on Crown land is unjust, I would remind them that as a citizen and landowner who holds title to his land and the mineral rights, I personally would receive a 1216 per cent share of any oil or gas discovered on my lands in Ontario. Why should it be any different for all Canadians, on all Crown land that is owned by Canada and Canadians?
I remind the members of this chamber that it was in my constituency of Lambton-Middlesex where oil was first discovered in North America, at Oil Springs, Ontario. In fact, Imperial Oil Company was first established in the town of Petrolia, later to move to Sarnia and then expand to its current status. Some of those old wells are over 100 years old and are still producing. Further exploration is continuing and seismic work is being done. 1 witnessed a rig that was moved to a new site in Sombre township last Sunday morning. The point I am making is that this region, very small though it may be, in comparison to the vastness of the area that would be under the jurisdiction of this act, this original oil field has been producing for more than 100 years, and exploration work is still going on.
There is continuing interest in the Silerian Reef formation that covers the eastern part of the state of Michigan and southwestern Ontario. New wells are being found at varying levels and pinnacle peaks and salt domes are being sought. One particularly interesting area is the offshore regions in Lake Erie, and, although natural gas was discovered there many years ago, new wells are being discovered in new areas where it was previously thought none had existed.
But like other offshore discoveries of greater magnitude, such as Hibernia or the Beaufort Sea, new technology has enabled the drillers to locate those fields by using shock waves or seismic. On land, small shallow holes are drilled, small explosive charges are placed and listening devices wired in sequence. As these explosive charges are detonated in series, shock waves echo back from rock formation below, indicating depths of domes and basins far below. Similar apparatus is towed behind ships, and by using small compressed air explosions in the water, science has enabled us to identify similar domes and basins below the ocean floor.
When an abnormal formation is discovered, a grid pattern of seismic sounds is applied to identify the extent of those structures below and to determine the best location to drill a well.
In the act before us today, there is a definition included to ensure it is clearly understood that a significant find or discovery is one well, but a commercial discovery is more than one or a series of wells. Provision is included in this act in clause 44 to give the minister authority to make a declaration of that significant discovery in respect to these lands, and any adjacent lands where he has reason to believe the significant discovery may extend.
In clauses 45, 46 and 47 the minister may make declarations of commercial discoveries and order additional wells to be drilled on the relevant Canada lands at such time and places as the minister should indicate. In other words, if a company finds an oil or gas field on Crown lands, this gives the authority to the minister to ensure that Canadians know the size of the discovery and the extent of the region and the potential production.
This legislation relates to the minister. Most acts do relate to ministers, but while they do have authority, it is usual that that authority is delegated to other bodies. In spite of the fact that those other bodies may make decisions, the ultimate responsibility rests with ministers. It is not unusual in legislation to relate authority to those who have responsibility. Even though they may have other bodies under their jurisdiction, ministers still have the responsibility and have to live up to it.
Clause 48 ensures that the power is included in the act to order that production commence at the times and places and in the quantities specified in the order and that sales are made to specified persons and at prices specified in the order. By the same token, power is included to stop or suspend production for periods of time specified in the order. This provides an assurance to us that a large discovery will be brought to the
January 15, 1981

attention of the Canadian people and that some large company cannot sit on a large discovery and say, "When you increase the price by so much we will start producing" or in other terms, "If you do not do certain things we will cut back by 15 per cent". We want to protect the people of Canada against such actions as this.
The last clause upon which I want to touch is clause 49 and the establishment of a revolving fund to ensure that proper environmental studies are conducted prior to the start of exploration work on the impact on our ecology during the drilling, development and producing stages in these highly sensitive regions of our environment.
I am well aware of the consequences in my own constituency when a dry hole is drilled and not properly plugged. There are hundreds of these in Lambton county. There are old wells from the 1800s which are no longer producing and which have been abandoned but left unplugged. They have since contaminated surrounding water wells because oil has come up to the water level in those wells and spread out through water veins. These unplugged abandoned wells have made it impossible to use modern further recovery techniques in these fields, and I refer to the fact that it is no longer possible to pressurize these rock formations. If we could pressurize these old formations, we could force out tens of thousands of barrels of oil which still exist in these fields. 1 am also aware of the damage this can cause to lands adjacent to a well or an oil field not only because of oil spills but also because of mud pits used in the drilling process and because of pipeline construction.
Just recently a constituent came to me regarding three very large gas transmission lines which cross his farm. Not only was there a tremendous displacement and loss of topsoil during the installation of these lines, but my constituent's whole underground tile drainage system was affected. Mr. Miseck lost a strip of land. If proper procedures and studies had taken place prior to that installation, the result would have been known and the land would have been restored to its productive potential. This was as recent as the 1950s, 1960s and early 1970s. This was in the province of Ontario. This type of environmental damage is much different from that found on Crown lands. We must be ever cognizant of the fragility of the ecology of the north, of the marine life in our offshore waters and the impact on our fishing industry, not just next year or the year after but ten or 20 years from now.
1 have a particular interest in this area because of another situation in my own neighbourhood. A well was being drilled last summer and, in spite of all normal precautions and additional expertise flown in from western Canada, as the normal depths were approached a salt dome was penetrated, and the ensuing flow of brine saturated the site and may result in soil damage to land around that rig which may take years to recover.
In spite of modern technology and normal precautions on two of the best farms in Canada, which are less than five miles apart in my own neighbourhood both Mr. Miseck and Mr. Williams have incurred damage which may lower the productivity of the land for years to come. While these two cases do
Canada Oil and Gas Act
not come under the jurisdiction of the National Energy Board or the Department of the Environment, I am pleased that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) has the foresight to ensure that this does not happen on Crown lands, or, if it does happen, that absolute liability is assessed against the operators.
Naturally I am interested in ensuring that adequate precautions are taken, and 1 will be watching with interest what happens this spring as drilling resumes in my own area. I understand that five wells have been planned for my area for this coming year. These will be drilled by Canadian drilling companies which have not been discouraged or affected by the national energy policy and which have chosen to remain in Canada as responsible corporate citizens to work toward Canadian self-sufficiency. In fact, some of the preliminary work was a joint effort by a very large multinational company and a very small Canadian company.
If five of the very largest multinational companies can accept the restrictions placed on their operations by some of the nations to which I referred earlier, then 1 can see no reason why they cannot operate here in Canada as we work toward our objectives in the interests of all Canadians. Of course, very large corporations-I refer to Exxon, Shell, British Petroleum, Mobil, Gulf, Texaco and I could go on-would object to any change in direction of Canadian policy or any policy which would lower their profits in any country. As we are all aware, these profits have increased dramatically over the last few years. A policy which would increase Canadian control and ownership of our resources had to be implemented to secure these resources for our future.
It has been ten years since the industry was advised that the regime for the disposition of oil and gas rights in the frontier regions, the offshore and the territories would be extensively revised. This new Canada oil and gas act was originally introduced in the House as Bill C-20 on December 20, 1977. The bill before us tonight for second reading is needed both from the industry's standpoint and from the regulatory standpoint. From the industry's standpoint we must establish certainty as to the tenure of gas and oil rights in the fiscal regime, thus providing for a stable investment climate. The industry will know precisely where it stands. From a Canadian standpoint this legislation is required to lay down more specific rules and guidelines as we move toward our objective of increased Canadian ownership and security of supply.
I indicated earlier that I come from the oldest oil producing region of North America. 1 have grown up in the midst of that industry. I saw the phasing out of the old Canadian Oil Company refinery at Petrolia, Ontario. It built a new facility at Sarnia which was later bought by Shell just 15 or 20 years ago. Then we saw the establishment of the Sun Oil refinery at Sarnia next to the Imperial Oil refinery. This region became known as the "Chemical Valley", and a fleet of tanker trucks collected the oil from the surrounding oil fields and delivered it to these refineries.
Since those earlier pioneer days pollution has been a problem. Tremendous strides have been made to correct this, to

January 15, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
eliminate the possibility of oil spills, to locate and plug old abandoned wells and to fill in old underground storage pits where crude oil was originally stored while it awaited refining. But this has happened over several decades. Now, as technology has advanced and people have become aware of environmental damage the same risk is not there. This legislation provides the necessary power to conduct environmental studies. As I indicated earlier, we intend to avoid the mistakes made by the early pioneers. We are placing total liability on the shoulders of the operator. In this context the legislation is clear, concise and simple. I endorse and support this legislation. It does not impose the stringent financial burdens on companies as the other oil producing nations to which I referred earlier do. This legislation reflects and fulfils the needs of the people of Canada. It has placed the emphasis on an early assessment of the oil and gas potential of our frontier regions, but this requirement will not be fulfilled at the expense of the fisheries or the environment. It is the intent of the legislation that proper assessments be made of environmental damage potential and then that the recommendations and findings of those assessments are adhered to. This legislation will be of benefit to all Canadians.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on Bill C-48, an act to regulate oil and gas interests in Canada lands and to amend the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act, because of the impact of this legislation on my native province of Nova Scotia.
When the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) introduced this bill on December 11, 1980, he called it a key element in the successful fulfilment of the government's national energy program. In his words, this bill:
-will establish a new and modernized regime to govern resources development activity in those immense frontier regions of our country known as the Canada lands.
He went on to say:
Our offshore regions cover an area of some 2.5 million square miles. The territories alone comprise another 1.5 million square miles. Together this is what we call the Canada lands, an area which is almost twice the size of the ten provinces combined.
Then the minister, warming up to his subject, claimed:
The promise of this vast frontier region is as enormous as its size. It represents Canada's best prospects for large, new reserves of conventional petroleum. It holds the key to our energy security .. .
Oil and gas rights have already been issued for 350 million acres in the Canada lands. Virtually all the area is considered promising in terms of potential reserves. Bill C-48 will convert these existings rights to the new land management regime thereby establishing it in a meaningful way.
We must ask how is this rich prize to be taken over. The minister left nothing to the imagination as he outlined his government's plans under seven major headings. I think it is only fitting that I repeat them because there is some misunderstanding as to why we are objecting to this legislation. The minister stated:
First, there will be stiffer work requirements through negotiated exploration agreements which include firm drilling commitments. Second, we will reserve to
the Crown a 25 per cent share of oil and gas rights in the Canada lands, to be exercised through Petro-Canada or some other designated Crown corporation.
I guess that means more bureaucracy, Mr. Speaker, and more Crown corporations. The minister went on:
Third, there will be a minimum requirement of 50 per cent Canadian ownership, through the private or public sector, of production from the Canada lands. Fourth, we will ensure optimum employment of Canadians, and the use of Canadian goods and services in oil and gas activities carried out on the Canada lands. Fifth, we will provide ministerial authority to order production to commence and be delivered to Canadian markets in quantities and at prices specified in the order. Sixth, we will be providing a greater degree of control in the timing, direction, rate and level of exploration, development and production by various means. These would include drilling and production orders, earlier release of proprietory information, prior approval of transfers and assigment of rights. Seventh, we will ensure that Canadians receive a fair return for their oil and gas resources through a basic royalty of 10 per cent, with an additional royalty of 40 per cent of the net profits of a field.
This is, of course, a very tall order. The minister also stated:
-the Canada oil and gas act will bring existing oil and gas rights into line with the new regime, but in such a way as to ensure that if these rights are not actively developed they will be relinquished to the Crown. Existing permits, leases and agreements will cither be converted to new leases and agreements within a year-
Only one year, Mr. Speaker.
-or will be surrendered to the Crown. Under the new regime, all exploration rights will lead to one type of production right only, namely, a production licence.
I have listened attentively to many of the speeches that were made, as well as to the minister when he made his initial speech, and I say to you, sir, that this bill makes a mockery of parliamentary democracy. You will note that when I listed the seven major headings as stated by the minister in the House, he kept saying "we will do this", "we will do that", "we will ensure", "we will provide". It is not Parliament, not the private sector that will do this, nor the peoples' representatives but the minister, whose background in the oil industry leaves much to be desired and is far from impressive, who will decide. Is it any wonder that when these proposals became known to the public, the oil, gas and well drilling companies started to leave Canada in droves? Instead of welcoming the minister's national energy plan, the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada, in full page advertisements in several of our daily newspapers right across the land levelled forceful criticism at the minister and the government saying that his proposals will only hurt Canadians by raising fuel prices, by making Canadians more dependent on expensive and insecure foreign oil. They said it will delay essential frontier exploration as well as oil sands plants and heavy oil development, it will cost Canadians more for gasoline and heating oil in the long run, and it will cost thousands of jobs which would be created by the oil industry right across Canada. The independent Canadian companies stated "we are the people your program was supposed to help, but it doesn't help us at all, it has stopped us in our tracks".
This policy, Mr. Speaker, has not only stopped the independent oil companies in their tracks. I say through you, sir, to the minister, that it appears to have stopped development and progress in all of Canada. All you need to do is look
January 15, 1981

at the daily statistics that are being supplied. The minister, however, only laughs off these criticisms saying they are nothing to be concerned about, they are merely the big crocodile tears of the vast oil interests in Canada. I ask the minister, who is in his seat in the House today, whether he shares the opinion of Mr. Rowland Frazee, chairman of the Royal Bank, who stated in Montreal, on January 8, 1981, that the federal government should scrap its national energy program and concentrate on drawing up a new policy rather than worrying about the constitution. In the words of Mr. Frazee: "It seems abundantly clear by now that the national energy program is so seriously flawed as to be a non-starter, which should be withdrawn and reconsidered! Canada's number one energy priority should be self-sufficiency in oil, but 'high noon' confrontations between the federal government and the provinces are blocking progress". These are the words of the chief executive of one of Canada's biggest banks, but I doubt whether his advice and his suggestions will meet with any more acceptance by the minister than do the carefully worded suggestions and recommendations made by members of Parliament from this side of the House. It is somewhat like the words of the mother watching the parade go by, turning to dad and saying, "You know, dear, everyone is out of step but our John." That is the attitude of this minister. Obviously, the moves being made by the minister against foreign investment in his attempts to gain great Canadian ownership of the oil industry can only further damage Canada's reputation abroad and cause wasteful bickering at home. I say to the minister, through you, sir, that if he continues to pursue the policies as outlined in this bill, we will continue to see more projects delayed or go down the drain or, more accurately go down south. We will see the Canadian dollar fall still further. We will see the price which we paid for our imports increasing and our inflation continuing its upward spiral.
The clauses and proposals in this bill will never, 1 submit, help us to settle our domestic problems or our international difficulties. In my opinion, this government's inability to see the tremendous potential of this nation is undoubtedly its greatest weakness. This government, with its preoccupation for the acquisition of still greater power, with its determination to still further socialize Canadian industry and build an even greater bureaucracy is, unfortunately, causing all Canadians to forfeit their opportunity to build on our strengths for the future. That is the crime of this type of legislation. The minister has carefully detailed the powers and the privileges which he considers essential to be retained by the federal government under this bill for control of the Canada lands. Some still ask, "What are these lands?" In fact only a moment ago 1 placed a question, at his consent, before the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) for whom 1 have a great deal of respect. In his answer he seemed to state that there was nothing about the ownership of lands to which I referred in the bill. 1 regret that he has not read his own government's "National Energy Program" of 1980, for, if he had, he would see what the minister is talking about when he speaks of Canada lands. They include all of the Yukon, all of the
Canada Oil and Gas Act
Northwest Territories, the Labrador Shelf, the Grand Banks, all of the Scotian shelf which includes Sable Island and the area adjacent to New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. That is what they intend to take, to rape from the rest of Canada through this type of legislation.
As a Nova Scotian I believe it is my duty and responsibility to place on the record the position of those I represent so that the minister and the government can evaluate the different points of view and hopefully through debate and discussion resolve the different problems facing both governments on this matter.
The exploitation of offshore oil and gas could be the most important commercial development of the twentieth century for Nova Scotia. Offshore oil and gas could give Nova Scotians the financial resources to attack deeply-rooted economic problems and strengthen weaker sectors of the economy. In our view it is a real chance for those of us who live in Nova Scotia.
Oil and gas production from our own fields would also provide badly needed independence from our presently insecure supply of increasingly costly oil imports. At present all the oil consumed in my province of Nova Scotia is foreign-pro-duced and large federal payments are needed to maintain a uniform Canadian oil price to consumers. Reducing or eliminating oil imports would improve Canada's balance of payments and stabilize the cost of oil to Canadian consumers.
We realize as well that offshore oil and gas developments could also present problems if they are not properly managed and controlled. Experience in other jurisdictions shows us that large oil and gas developments can be highly disruptive. They can lead to inflation because the funds involved are so large in relation to the rest of the economy. They can disturb living patterns, for example, by causing real estate prices to soar. They can also harm the environment, a fact which has been mentioned earlier in the House and is well-known to all Nova Scotians who sadly remember and will never forget the disastrous Arrow and Kurdistan spills off their shores. Offshore oil and gas developments can overwhelm long-established local industries and small businesses, unless these firms can plan carefully with government guidance and protection to get their share of the action.
As Nova Scotians we believe strongly that the regulators and decision makers must have the closest possible direct links to the communities involved and be responsible solely to the jurisdiction most affected. This is one of the key reasons Nova Scotia insists it would be folly to allow the control and management of the offshore resources of the province to slip away from provincial hands.
Nova Scotia has already passed legislation to ensure that oil and gas activities, on and off the shores of the province, will provide the optimum benefit to Nova Scotians. In four separate acts provision is made by the government of Nova Scotia to determine the extent of employment of Nova Scotian workers and the use of Nova Scotian goods and services in all

January 15, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Ad
phases of exploration, development and production. Provision is made for regulations regarding education and training of Nova Scotians to enable them to participate in the many job opportunities which these developments will generate.
Finally, provision is made for the establishment of compensation funds to reimburse individuals who might suffer loss as a result of exploitation and development as well as pipeline or gas utility activities. 1 hope the House will realize that Nova Scotia has a strong and positive legal claim for ownership and control of its offshore resources. 1 repeat what I stated a moment ago in the form of a question in the House. Our claim goes back as far as 1621 when King James I granted the Royal Charter of Nova Scotia to Sir William Alexander. In recognition of the utter dependence of the early colonists-and of course this applies to the people who settled in my home town of Lunenburg-the water adjacent to our shores was granted to the province since the food the colonists required and the transportation mode was all by sea. In recognition of this dependence the king included as part of our territory a band of sea stretching about 120 miles southward from our coasts. This band easily encompasses Sable Island. That is why if Your Honour lived on Sable Island and an election was called-I am not certain how you would vote-you would be required to vote in a Nova Scotia constituency and your ballot would be counted in the Halifax riding. This band which the king granted to Nova Scotia in 1621 includes Sable Island, a large share of the controversial Georges Bank, as well as most of the Scotian shelf. These boundaries were observed for many years despite numerous conquests and treaty settlements. In fact, Canada's constitution, the British North America Act of 1867, provided that Nova Scotia's limits would be exactly the same after as before Confederation.
I think it only fitting that I remind the House the international boundaries of Canada have remained fairly constant since Confederation, but within Canada there have been many changes. As federal territories in the west and north acquired value, either through settlement or mineral development, they were regularly and without question granted to the appropriate provinces. In fact Nova Scotia, as a result of its pre-confederation division into Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, is perhaps the only province in Canada which has grown smaller over the years.
For many years Ontario has asserted ownership and control over its minerals, as we have just heard from the last speaker, including oil and gas under the waters of the Great Lakes, and for the last two decades it has benefited from natural gas production in Lake Erie. These gas fields stretch southward nearly to the international boundary which exists between Canada and the United States. Nova Scotia sees no reason whatsoever why it should not have similar ownership of the resources which exist on its offshore banks. However, Nova Scotians believe that legal confrontation over the offshore jurisdictional question should only occur as a last resort. Once our views are fully known and understood, we are hopeful that our differences over these problems can be resolved through negotiation with the present federal government.
So there can be no misunderstanding, I wish to spell out the essential rights and powers which Nova Scotia must have to ensure that offshore development will be directed toward the benefit of Nova Scotia as well as Canada. These rights are exactly the same ones which are exerted by the provinces with respect to onshore resources. First, we believe Nova Scotia must have the power to control the pace of the development of its offshore resources in order to balance the possible formidable industrial expansion with the preservation of traditional social values and patterns. This requires that Nova Scotia have exclusive right to issue and set the conditions of all licences, leases and permits of all kinds, which relate to the exploration, development, production, transportation, refining and marketing of petroleum and petroleum products, subject only to the normal jurisdiction of the federal government in extra provincial trade.
Nova Scotia must have the right, sir, to a fair offshore resource royalty, rental and other revenue in order to fund education and training programs, to support administrative and regulatory agencies, to reverse the equalization payments system and to ensure that industrial activity in Nova Scotia is sustained after the offshore resources are depleted. Because of our high unemployment rate, Nova Scotia must have the ability to provide preferences for qualified Nova Scotian workers in the early years of development. This will be coupled with an intensive program of education and training, to bring as many as possible to the high standards required by this industry. Given moderate success offshore, it is expected that the need for these preferences will disappear within a very few years.
We also believe that Nova Scotia must be able to determine the conditions under which goods and services are supplied to industry operations, in order that Nova Scotia can obtain a share of these business activities-something we have sorely lacked for many years. Without some temporary preferences in the early stages of development, Nova Scotians will face extreme difficulty in entering the field against competition from large international firms. These rights and powers, when taken together, may seem to be comparable to ownership- without doubt, they constitute very substantial control of our offshore resources. However, ownership is not a precise term and there are many aspects of control other than those I have mentioned. Some are undeniably federal responsibilities; some are undeniably provincial responsibilities; and, of course, some are controversial, therefore, open to negotiation.
I believe prompt resolution of the controversial responsibilities is necessary in order to prevent delays in petroleum exploration off Nova Scotia's coast. I believe it can be achieved, either through constitutional amendments or within our existing constitutional framework. The Parliament of Canada, with the consent of Nova Scotia, has the authority to confirm by statute that our seaward boundaries are co-extensive with the boundaries of Canada for the purposes of resource exploration and development. The statute may

We in Nova Scotia hope our oil and gas potential can be developed; not through a process of confrontation, as appears to be the minister's position as outlined in Bill C-48, but rather through a process of consultation, which is the original manner in which the strength of our provinces was achieved and our nation developed. After all, sir, a chain is only as strong as its weakest link. Surely this government must eventually realize that legislation, which strengthens the economic position of our individual provinces, cannot help but strengthen the central government-and the nation. Unfortunately, Bill C-48 falls far short of its required goal. Instead of strengthening the provinces it seeks to take away more of their powers and concentrate that power in Ottawa. 1 say to you, sir, in conclusion, that this is a bad bill, an unjust bill. It does nothing to strengthen Canada and confederation. If the provinces are robbed of their resources they have nothing-nothing to work with, nothing on which to build. This is why I am opposed to this bill and why I intend to vote against it.
